biology-paper-1.title: Cell Structures and Microscopy
biology-paper-1.description: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, sub-cellular structures, and how microscopy reveals them.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
Eukaryotic and Prokaryotic Cells

All living organisms are made of cells. In OCR Gateway Science (B1.1), you need to understand two fundamental cell types: eukaryotic cells and prokaryotic cells.

Eukaryotic cells include animal and plant cells. They have a nucleus that encloses their genetic material within a nuclear membrane. They also contain membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells — such as bacteria — are much smaller and simpler. They lack a true nucleus; instead, their genetic material is a single loop of DNA floating freely in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes may also contain small rings of extra DNA called plasmids.

Key Fact

Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus that encloses their DNA. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus — their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and they may also contain plasmids.

Sub-cellular Structures and Their Functions

Both animal and plant cells are eukaryotic, but they contain different sub-cellular structures. The exam requires you to explain how each structure’s design relates to its function (B1.1b). This means you need to go beyond naming the structure — you must say why its shape, composition or position allows it to carry out its role efficiently.

Nucleus — contains the cell’s genetic material (chromosomes made of DNA) and controls the cell’s activities by determining which proteins are made. The nuclear membrane keeps the DNA separate from the cytoplasm, protecting the genetic code.

Cytoplasm — a jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions take place. Enzymes in the cytoplasm control these metabolic reactions. It also contains structural proteins that give the cell its shape.

Cell membrane — a thin, selectively permeable layer that controls which substances enter and leave the cell. It contains receptor molecules that allow the cell to respond to chemical signals such as hormones and neurotransmitters.

Mitochondria — the site of aerobic respiration. They contain the enzymes needed for cellular respiration and transfer energy for the cell’s processes. Cells with high energy demands (such as muscle cells) contain more mitochondria.

Ribosomes — tiny structures in the cytoplasm where protein synthesis occurs. They are found in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, though they are smaller in prokaryotes.

Plant cells have all the structures listed above, plus three additional ones that reflect their roles in photosynthesis and structural support:

Chloroplasts — contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. They absorb light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose. Chloroplasts are found mainly in leaf cells and cells near the surface of stems, where light is available.

Permanent vacuole — a large, fluid-filled space containing cell sap (a solution of sugars and salts dissolved in water). It helps maintain the cell’s rigidity by pressing the cytoplasm against the cell wall, keeping the cell turgid and supporting the plant structure.

Cell wall — made of cellulose and surrounds the cell membrane. It strengthens and supports the cell, preventing it from bursting when water enters by osmosis. Unlike the cell membrane, the cell wall is fully permeable and allows all dissolved substances through.

Key Fact

Plant cells have a cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a permanent vacuole (cell sap) in addition to animal cell organelles. Bacterial cells have a cell wall, but no chloroplasts, no true nucleus and no mitochondria.

Microscopy

Microscopes allow us to see cells and sub-cellular structures invisible to the naked eye. You need to know about light microscopes and electron microscopes (B1.1a, B1.1c).

Light microscopes use glass lenses and visible light. They have a useful magnification of about \(\times 1500\) and a resolution of around 200 nm. To prepare a slide, place a thin sample on a glass slide, add a drop of stain (such as iodine or methylene blue) to make colourless structures visible, then lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.

The OCR spec references practical work with light microscopes (PAG B1). You should be able to describe how to prepare slides, use staining techniques, and calculate magnification. Key steps:

1. Place a thin sample (e.g. onion epidermis or cheek cells) on a clean glass slide. 2. Add a drop of stain — iodine stains plant cell walls and nuclei yellow-brown, while methylene blue stains animal cell nuclei blue. 3. Gently lower a coverslip at 45° to avoid air bubbles. 4. Start on the lowest magnification objective lens, focus, then switch to higher magnifications.

To calculate the total magnification: \(\text{total magnification} = \text{eyepiece lens} \times \text{objective lens}\). For example, a \(\times 10\) eyepiece with a \(\times 40\) objective gives \(\times 400\) magnification.

Electron microscopes fire a beam of electrons at the specimen. A transmission electron microscope (TEM) has much higher resolution — down to about 0.2 nm — and a magnification of up to \(\times 2\,000\,000\). This allowed biologists to see sub-cellular structures like ribosomes and the internal folds of mitochondria (cristae) in fine detail, greatly increasing our understanding of how cells work (B1.1c).

The development of electron microscopy was a turning point in biology. Before electron microscopes, scientists could see cells and nuclei with light microscopes, but they could not resolve the detailed internal structure of organelles. Electron microscopy revealed that mitochondria have folded inner membranes (cristae) that increase the surface area for respiration enzymes, explaining why mitochondria are so efficient at energy transfer.

Key Fact

The magnification formula: \(\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{real size}}\). Always ensure both measurements are in the same units before calculating. Electron microscopes have much higher resolution (~0.2 nm) than light microscopes (~200 nm), allowing sub-cellular detail to be seen.

biology-paper-1.title: Cell Chemistry and Enzymes
biology-paper-1.description: DNA structure, protein synthesis basics, and how enzymes work as biological catalysts.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
DNA — The Code of Life

Inside every cell is DNA, the molecule that carries the genetic instructions for building and running an organism. For OCR Gateway B1.2, you need to understand DNA’s structure and how it leads to protein production.

DNA is a polymer — a long molecule made of many repeating sub-units called nucleotides. It consists of two strands twisted around each other to form a double helix. The strands are held together by pairs of complementary bases. There are four bases in DNA, and they always pair in the same way: adenine (A) with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) with guanine (G). This is known as complementary base pairing.

The sequence of bases along the DNA acts as a code. Each group of three bases codes for a particular amino acid. This triplet code determines the order in which amino acids are assembled during protein synthesis at the ribosomes. Different sequences of amino acids produce different proteins, each with a unique shape and function.

Key Fact

DNA is a polymer made of two strands forming a double helix. The sequence of bases along the DNA provides a code that determines the order of amino acids assembled into proteins at the ribosomes.

From DNA to Protein

The journey from gene to protein involves two key stages. First, in the nucleus, the relevant section of DNA is used as a template to produce a molecule of mRNA (messenger RNA). This mRNA carries the copied code out of the nucleus and into the cytoplasm. Second, at the ribosomes, the code on the mRNA is read and used to assemble amino acids in the correct order. The resulting chain of amino acids folds into a specific 3D shape, forming a functional protein.

Proteins are essential for life. They include enzymes (biological catalysts), structural proteins (such as collagen and keratin), hormones (such as insulin), and antibodies (part of the immune system). Because the DNA base sequence determines which proteins are made, DNA ultimately controls the cell’s characteristics and functions.

Enzymes — Biological Catalysts

Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, speeding up the chemical reactions that occur inside cells without being used up themselves. They play a central role in metabolism — the sum of all chemical reactions in a cell. Without enzymes, metabolic reactions would be too slow to sustain life.

Each enzyme has a uniquely shaped region called the active site. Only a substrate with the correct complementary shape can fit into the active site, like a key fitting into a lock. This is the lock and key hypothesis. When the substrate binds, the enzyme-substrate complex forms, the enzyme catalyses the reaction, and the products are released. The enzyme is then free to accept another substrate molecule.

Temperature — as temperature increases, molecules move faster and collide more frequently with the enzyme, increasing the rate of reaction. However, above the optimum temperature, the enzyme begins to denature — the bonds holding the active site in shape break, the active site changes shape, and the substrate can no longer fit. The reaction rate drops sharply. It is important to note that different enzymes have different optimum temperatures — not all enzymes work best at 37°C.

pH — each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works fastest. For most human enzymes this is around pH 7 (neutral), but pepsin in the stomach works best at pH 2 (acidic). Moving away from the optimum causes the active site to change shape, reducing activity. Extreme pH values cause permanent denaturation.

Substrate concentration — increasing substrate concentration increases the rate because more substrate molecules collide with enzyme active sites per unit time. Eventually, all active sites are occupied simultaneously (the enzyme is saturated) and the rate plateaus — adding more substrate has no further effect.

Enzyme concentration — more enzyme molecules mean more active sites available, so the rate increases (assuming there is excess substrate to bind to them).

Key Fact

Enzymes have a specific active site that fits only one substrate (lock and key). Above the optimum temperature or at extreme pH, the active site changes shape permanently — the enzyme is denatured and can no longer catalyse the reaction.

A common practical involves testing the effect of amylase on starch (B1.2c). Amylase is a digestive enzyme that breaks down starch into simpler sugars (maltose). You can monitor this reaction by taking samples at regular intervals and testing with iodine solution — the iodine turns blue-black when starch is present, but stays brown-orange once the starch has been fully digested.

To investigate the effect of temperature, set up water baths at different temperatures (e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60°C). Place test tubes containing amylase and starch in each water bath, allow them to equilibrate, then mix and start timing. Sample at regular intervals and test with iodine. Record the time taken for starch to be fully digested at each temperature.

To calculate the rate of reaction: \(\text{rate} = \frac{1}{\text{time}}\). A shorter time means a faster rate. Plot rate against temperature to find the optimum. Control variables include the volume and concentration of amylase and starch, and the pH of the buffer solution.

Understanding enzyme-controlled reactions is fundamental to biology. Enzymes control digestion (amylase, protease, lipase break down food), respiration (enzymes in mitochondria transfer energy from glucose), photosynthesis (enzymes in chloroplasts fix carbon dioxide) and protein synthesis (enzymes help assemble amino acids).

In industry, enzymes are used in biological washing powders (proteases and lipases break down stains at lower temperatures, saving energy), food production (e.g. isomerase converts glucose to fructose for slimming foods), and brewing (yeast enzymes ferment sugars into ethanol). Their specificity and efficiency make them invaluable tools.

biology-paper-1.title: Respiration
biology-paper-1.description: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration, energy transfer, and the synthesis of biological molecules.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
What is Cellular Respiration?

Cellular respiration is a chemical process that occurs continuously in every living cell — animals, plants, fungi and bacteria all respire. It is not the same as breathing (ventilation) — respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells that transfers energy from glucose to a molecule called ATP. This energy drives all life processes, from muscle contraction and nerve impulse transmission to protein synthesis and active transport (B1.3a).

Respiration is an exothermic reaction — it transfers energy to the surroundings, which is why your body feels warm (B1.3b). This transferred energy is vital: without it, cells could not carry out any of their functions.

Key Fact

Cellular respiration is a universal, exothermic chemical process that occurs continuously in all living cells. It transfers energy from glucose to ATP. It is NOT breathing.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and occurs in the mitochondria. It produces a large yield of ATP, making it the most efficient form of respiration. This is why organisms with high energy demands (like mammals) rely primarily on aerobic respiration.

The word equation is:

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$

The balanced symbol equation: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\)

Notice that glucose is completely broken down in aerobic respiration. All the chemical energy stored in the glucose molecule is transferred — some to ATP for cellular work, and some as heat to the surroundings. This complete breakdown is why aerobic respiration releases much more ATP than anaerobic respiration.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is not available (or in short supply), for example during intense exercise when the blood cannot deliver oxygen fast enough to muscles. It takes place in the cytoplasm and produces much less ATP than aerobic respiration because glucose is only partially broken down (B1.3c).

In animal cells: \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}\)

The incomplete breakdown of glucose produces lactic acid, which builds up in muscles during intense exercise, causing cramps and fatigue. After exercise, the body needs extra oxygen to break down the accumulated lactic acid — this is called the oxygen debt. You continue to breathe heavily after exercise to repay this debt: the extra oxygen is used to oxidise lactic acid in the liver, converting it back to glucose.

In plants and fungi: \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}\)

This process is called fermentation. It is used commercially in brewing (yeast produces ethanol for alcoholic drinks) and bread-making (yeast produces carbon dioxide that makes dough rise; the ethanol evaporates during baking). Note that plants can also carry out anaerobic respiration producing lactic acid in waterlogged roots, but the fungal/yeast pathway is the one most commonly examined.

Key Fact

Aerobic respiration (with oxygen, in mitochondria) produces a large yield of ATP. Anaerobic respiration (without oxygen, in cytoplasm) produces much less ATP. In animals it makes lactic acid; in fungi and plants it makes ethanol and carbon dioxide.

Biological Molecules

Respiration links to the synthesis and breakdown of key biological molecules. You need to understand the role of sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol as building blocks (B1.3d–f).

Carbohydrates: Simple sugars (monomers) such as glucose join together to form complex carbohydrates (polymers such as starch and glycogen). Glucose is the key monomer used in respiration. Starch is the storage form of glucose in plants; glycogen is the storage form in animals (stored in the liver and muscles).

Proteins: Amino acid monomers join together in specific sequences (determined by DNA) to form protein polymers. Proteins are essential for enzymes, structural components (collagen, keratin), hormones (insulin) and antibodies. The sequence and type of amino acids determines the protein’s shape and function.

Lipids: Formed from fatty acids and glycerol. Lipids are used for long-term energy storage (they contain more energy per gram than carbohydrates), thermal insulation, and making cell membranes. Lipids are not polymers in the strict sense because they are not made of repeating identical monomers.

The energy transferred by respiration is used to build these molecules as well as break them down. For example, energy from respiration drives the synthesis of proteins from amino acids, and the conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage. When the body needs energy, glycogen is broken back down into glucose for respiration.

Exercise and Respiration

During exercise, your muscles need more energy, so the rate of respiration increases. Your body responds by increasing heart rate (to deliver more oxygenated blood to muscles), increasing breathing rate and depth (to take in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide), and breaking down glycogen stored in muscles and the liver into glucose. If exercise is intense enough that the blood cannot supply oxygen fast enough, muscles switch to anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid. After exercise stops, you continue breathing heavily to supply the extra oxygen needed to break down lactic acid in the liver — this is the oxygen debt.

You can test for the products of respiration experimentally. Breathing out through limewater turns it milky, confirming the presence of carbon dioxide. Using a temperature probe in a flask of germinating seeds shows a temperature increase over time, confirming that respiration is exothermic.

biology-paper-1.title: Photosynthesis
biology-paper-1.description: How plants use light energy to convert CO2 and water into glucose and oxygen.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
What is Photosynthesis?

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and algae produce food. They are the main producers of biomass for life on Earth — almost all food chains begin with a photosynthetic organism (B1.4a). Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy.

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction — it takes in energy from the surroundings in the form of light (B1.4c). This is the opposite of respiration, which is exothermic. The word equation:

$$\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$$

The balanced symbol equation: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{light}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\)

The OCR spec describes photosynthesis as a two-stage process (B1.4b). In the first stage, light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and used to split water molecules, releasing oxygen as a by-product. In the second stage, the hydrogen from water is combined with carbon dioxide to produce glucose. Both stages occur in the chloroplasts.

Key Fact

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in chloroplasts: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll. It is a two-stage process: light splits water, then hydrogen combines with CO\(_2\) to make glucose.

What Happens to the Glucose?

Glucose produced by photosynthesis has several important uses in the plant:

Respiration — glucose is broken down to transfer energy for the plant’s life processes. Starch storage — excess glucose is converted to insoluble starch for storage (starch does not affect osmosis because it is insoluble). Cellulose — glucose is converted to cellulose for building cell walls. Amino acids and proteins — glucose is combined with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil to make amino acids, which are assembled into proteins. Lipids — glucose can be converted to lipids (fats and oils) for energy storage in seeds.

Factors Affecting the Rate of Photosynthesis

Three main factors affect the rate: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature (B1.4e). Each can become a limiting factor — the factor in shortest supply that prevents the rate from increasing.

Light intensity — as light intensity increases, the rate increases because more energy is available for the light-dependent stage. At high intensity, the rate levels off because CO\(_2\) concentration or temperature becomes the limiting factor. The inverse square law applies: \(\text{light intensity} \propto \frac{1}{\text{distance}^2}\). Doubling the distance from a light source quarters the intensity.

Carbon dioxide concentration — increasing CO\(_2\) provides more raw material for the carbon fixation stage, so the rate increases. Eventually, the rate plateaus when another factor (light or temperature) becomes limiting. In commercial greenhouses, farmers pump in extra CO\(_2\) to maximise crop yields.

Temperature — enzymes controlling photosynthesis work faster as temperature increases up to an optimum (typically around 25–30°C for many plants). Above this, enzymes denature and the rate drops sharply. Below the optimum, molecules have less kinetic energy and collide less frequently with enzyme active sites.

The three factors interact (B1.4f, Higher Tier). On a graph of rate vs. light intensity, you might see the rate plateau even though light is still increasing — this means CO\(_2\) or temperature is now the limiting factor. To increase the rate further, you would need to increase whichever factor is limiting. All three must be sufficient for the maximum rate to be achieved.

Key Fact

A limiting factor is the one in shortest supply preventing the rate from increasing further. On a graph, it shows as a plateau. The three limiting factors interact — all must be sufficient for maximum rate.

A common practical uses Cabomba (pondweed) or Elodea. Place the pondweed underwater in a beaker with a lamp nearby and count oxygen bubbles produced per minute at different distances from the lamp. As the lamp moves further away, light intensity decreases (inverse square law) and fewer bubbles are produced, indicating a lower rate of photosynthesis.

For more accurate results, collect the gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder over water and measure the volume per unit time, rather than counting individual bubbles. Repeat each distance at least three times and calculate a mean to improve reliability.

You can also test leaves for starch using iodine solution (B1.4d): boil the leaf in water to kill the cells, then in ethanol to remove chlorophyll (the green colour), rinse in water, and add iodine. Blue-black = starch present (photosynthesis occurred). Brown-orange = no starch (no photosynthesis). This test can show which parts of a variegated leaf photosynthesise (only the green parts).

Farmers and horticulturalists use their understanding of limiting factors to maximise crop yields in greenhouses. They may use artificial lighting to extend the growing day, add CO\(_2\) from gas burners, and control temperature with heaters or ventilation. The cost of these measures must be balanced against the extra income from improved yields — there is no point adding expensive lighting if CO\(_2\) is the limiting factor.

biology-paper-1.title: Supplying the Cell and Challenges of Size
biology-paper-1.description: Diffusion, osmosis, active transport, and why multicellular organisms need transport systems.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
Moving Substances Into and Out of Cells

Cells need to transport substances across their membranes to survive. There are three main mechanisms: diffusion, osmosis and active transport (B2.1a).

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration — it is passive (no energy needed). Oxygen diffuses into cells for respiration; carbon dioxide and urea diffuse out. The steeper the concentration gradient, the faster the rate of diffusion. Temperature and surface area also affect the rate — higher temperature means faster-moving particles and more frequent collisions.

Osmosis is specifically the movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a more concentrated one (low water potential). The OCR spec uses the term water potential but does not require mathematical calculations with it.

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. This requires energy from respiration. Root hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil, where the concentration of minerals is lower than inside the cell. The energy comes from ATP produced by mitochondria in the root hair cells.

Key Fact

Diffusion and osmosis are passive processes (no energy needed). Active transport requires energy from respiration to move substances against the concentration gradient, from low to high concentration.

The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

Cells divide to produce new cells for growth, repair and replacement of damaged tissue. The cell cycle has several stages (B2.1b): first the cell grows and increases in size, then the DNA replicates so there are two copies of every chromosome, the cell grows a little more, and finally it divides by mitosis. Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.

Differentiation is the process by which a cell becomes specialised to perform a particular function (B2.1c). Specialised cells have specific structures suited to their role, making the organism more efficient. For example, red blood cells are biconcave with no nucleus to maximise space for haemoglobin; nerve cells have long axons to transmit impulses over distance; root hair cells have extensions to increase surface area for absorption.

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and produce different cell types (B2.1d–f). Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into any cell type in the body, making them potentially useful for treating diseases. Adult stem cells (e.g. in bone marrow) can only produce a limited range of cell types, such as blood cells. Meristems in plants contain stem cells that allow plants to continue growing and differentiating throughout their lives — unlike most animal cells, which lose the ability to differentiate early in development.

The use of embryonic stem cells raises ethical questions because the embryo is destroyed in the process. Some people argue the medical benefits outweigh this concern; others oppose it on moral or religious grounds.

The Challenges of Size

As organisms get larger, their surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) decreases (B2.2a). Consider a cube: a 1 cm cube has a SA:V ratio of 6:1, while a 2 cm cube has a ratio of only 3:1. This means simple diffusion alone cannot supply enough substances or remove waste fast enough for large organisms. Multicellular organisms therefore need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems.

Humans have a double circulatory system (B2.2c): one circuit pumps blood from the heart to the lungs for gas exchange (pulmonary circuit), the other pumps oxygenated blood from the heart to the body and back (systemic circuit). This maintains high blood pressure for efficient delivery of oxygen and nutrients.

The heart has four chambers — two atria (receive blood) and two ventricles (pump blood out). The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall because it pumps blood further (around the whole body). Valves prevent backflow and ensure blood flows in one direction (B2.2d).

Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure (thick muscular walls, small lumen, elastic fibres). Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure (thinner walls, larger lumen, valves to prevent backflow). Capillaries are tiny vessels with walls just one cell thick, allowing efficient exchange of substances by diffusion between the blood and surrounding tissues (B2.2d).

Red blood cells are biconcave discs with no nucleus, packed with haemoglobin to carry oxygen. Their biconcave shape increases surface area for oxygen absorption. Plasma is the liquid component of blood that transports dissolved substances including glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones, carbon dioxide and antibodies (B2.2e).

Key Fact

As organisms get larger, their surface area to volume ratio decreases. This is why multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (e.g. alveoli in lungs, villi in the intestine) and transport systems (e.g. the circulatory system) to move substances efficiently.

Root hair cells have long thin extensions that greatly increase the surface area for absorbing water (by osmosis) and mineral ions (by active transport) from the soil (B2.2f).

Xylem vessels transport water and dissolved minerals upwards from roots to leaves in a continuous column (B2.2h). Xylem cells are dead, hollow tubes reinforced with lignin (a waterproof, rigid material) that provides structural support. The movement of water through the plant is called the transpiration stream — water evaporates from the leaves through stomata, creating a “pull” that draws water up through the xylem (B2.2g).

Phloem tubes transport dissolved sugars (sucrose) from the leaves (where they are made by photosynthesis) to the rest of the plant — this is called translocation (B2.2g–h). Phloem cells are living and have sieve plates with tiny pores to allow movement of dissolved substances. Unlike xylem, translocation requires energy and can move substances both up and down the plant.

Environmental factors affect how quickly water is lost from leaves (B2.2i–j): light intensity (more light causes stomata to open wider), temperature (higher temperature increases evaporation rate), air movement/wind (blows away humid air from around the leaf, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient). A potometer is used to measure the rate of water uptake by a plant cutting, which is a proxy for transpiration rate.

biology-paper-1.title: The Nervous System
biology-paper-1.description: How the nervous system detects stimuli, transmits impulses and coordinates rapid responses.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
Structure of the Nervous System

The human nervous system allows the body to detect changes in the environment (stimuli) and produce rapid, coordinated responses (B3.1a). It consists of the central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord — and the peripheral nervous system — nerves that extend to all parts of the body, connecting the CNS to receptors and effectors.

The pathway for a nervous response involves a clear sequence: stimulus → sensory receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → motor neurone → effector (muscle or gland) → response.

The nervous system is able to coordinate responses because it has many links between different parts of the body, has different types of sensory receptors for different stimuli (light receptors in the eyes, temperature receptors in the skin, chemical receptors in the nose and tongue), and can process information in the CNS before sending out appropriate signals (B3.1b).

Key Fact

The nervous pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in CNS) → motor neurone → effector → response. The CNS (brain and spinal cord) processes information and coordinates the response.

Neurones and Their Structure

There are three types of neurone: sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS, relay neurones are found within the CNS and connect sensory neurones to motor neurones, and motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.

The OCR spec requires you to know the structure of sensory and motor neurones (B3.1b). Both have a cell body containing the nucleus, dendrites (short branches that receive impulses), and a long axon that transmits the electrical impulse. Motor neurones have a long axon running from the spinal cord to the effector. Sensory neurones have a long dendron connecting the receptor to the cell body, and a shorter axon entering the CNS. The axon may be insulated by a myelin sheath, which speeds up impulse transmission.

Synapses

Where two neurones meet there is a tiny gap called a synapse. The electrical impulse cannot cross this gap directly. Instead, when the impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone, chemicals called neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synaptic gap. These neurotransmitters diffuse across the gap and bind to specific receptor molecules on the membrane of the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse that continues along the pathway (B3.1b).

Synapses ensure impulses travel in one direction only (because neurotransmitters are only released from one side and receptors are only on the other). They also allow the nervous system to connect many different pathways — a single neurone can have synapses with multiple other neurones, enabling complex coordination.

A reflex arc is the pathway that produces a rapid, automatic, protective response (a reflex) without conscious thought (B3.1c). The pathway is: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in spinal cord, not the brain) → motor neurone → effector.

For example, touching a hot object: pain receptors in the skin detect heat → sensory neurone carries the impulse to the spinal cord → relay neurone passes it directly to a motor neurone → motor neurone stimulates the muscle (effector) in the arm to contract → hand is pulled away. This bypasses the brain, making the response faster and protecting the body from harm.

Reflexes are important because they are faster than voluntary responses (fewer synapses to cross and a shorter pathway through the spinal cord rather than the brain). They protect the body from damage before you are consciously aware of the danger. Other examples include the pupil reflex (pupil constricts in bright light to protect the retina) and the knee-jerk reflex.

Key Fact

Reflex arcs produce rapid, automatic responses that bypass the brain, going through the spinal cord instead. This makes reflexes faster and protects the body from danger. The pathway involves fewer synapses than a voluntary response.

The ruler drop test measures reaction time (B3.1c practical). One person holds a ruler vertically; the other places their thumb and finger at the 0 cm mark without touching the ruler. When the ruler is released without warning, the subject catches it as quickly as possible. The distance fallen is recorded — a shorter distance means a faster reaction time.

To improve reliability: repeat the test at least five times and calculate a mean, discard anomalous results, and ensure the same person drops the ruler each time. You can convert the distance to time using the equation: \(t = \sqrt{\frac{2d}{g}}\) where \(d\) is distance in metres and \(g\) is \(9.8 \text{ m/s}^2\). Variables that could affect reaction time include caffeine, tiredness, distractions and practice.

The nervous system and endocrine system both coordinate body functions, but they work differently. The nervous system transmits electrical impulses along neurones for fast, short-lived, precise responses (e.g. pulling your hand away from heat). The endocrine system uses chemical hormones carried in the blood for slower, longer-lasting, widespread responses (e.g. controlling blood glucose over hours). The next lesson covers the endocrine system in detail.

biology-paper-1.title: The Endocrine System
biology-paper-1.description: Hormonal coordination, the menstrual cycle, contraception, and plant hormones.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
The Endocrine System

The endocrine system uses chemical messengers called hormones to coordinate and control body functions (B3.2a). Unlike the nervous system, which produces fast, short-lived, precise responses via electrical impulses, the endocrine system produces slower, longer-lasting and more widespread responses.

Hormones are produced by endocrine glands and released directly into the blood, which transports them to their target organs. Each hormone has specific target cells with receptors that recognise it — only cells with the correct receptor will respond to a particular hormone. Key endocrine glands include the pituitary gland (often called the “master gland” because it controls other glands), the thyroid gland, the adrenal glands, the pancreas and the ovaries/testes.

Key Fact

The endocrine system uses hormones (chemical messengers) transported in the blood to target organs with specific receptors. Responses are slower but longer-lasting than the nervous system. The pituitary gland is the “master gland” that controls other endocrine glands.

Thyroxine is produced by the thyroid gland and controls metabolic rate — the speed of chemical reactions in cells. It is regulated by negative feedback (B3.2b, Higher Tier): when thyroxine levels are high, the pituitary gland reduces production of TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), which in turn causes the thyroid to produce less thyroxine. When thyroxine levels drop too low, the pituitary increases TSH, stimulating more thyroxine production. This feedback loop keeps thyroxine levels stable.

Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands (located on top of the kidneys) in response to stress, danger or excitement (B3.2b). It triggers the “fight or flight” response: heart rate increases, breathing rate increases, blood is diverted from the gut to the muscles, glycogen in the liver is converted to glucose for extra energy, and the pupils dilate. These changes prepare the body to respond quickly to a threat.

Hormones in Human Reproduction

The menstrual cycle is a roughly 28-day cycle controlled by four key hormones interacting through feedback mechanisms (B3.2c–d). Testosterone, produced by the testes, controls the development of male secondary sexual characteristics and sperm production.

The four hormones controlling the menstrual cycle are:

FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) — produced by the pituitary gland, stimulates the maturation of an egg in the ovary (inside a follicle). Oestrogen — produced by the ovaries, repairs and thickens the uterus lining after menstruation, inhibits further FSH production, and stimulates the release of LH. LH (luteinising hormone) — produced by the pituitary gland, a surge of LH triggers ovulation (release of the mature egg from the ovary, around day 14). Progesterone — produced by the empty follicle (now called the corpus luteum), maintains the thick uterus lining ready for implantation. If no fertilisation occurs, progesterone levels drop, the lining breaks down, and menstruation begins.

Key Fact

The menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH (matures egg), oestrogen (repairs lining, triggers LH), LH (triggers ovulation) and progesterone (maintains lining). These hormones interact in feedback loops over a ~28-day cycle.

Hormonal contraception (B3.2e) includes the combined pill (contains oestrogen and progesterone), the mini-pill (progesterone only), implants and injections. These work by maintaining high levels of oestrogen and/or progesterone, which inhibit FSH production from the pituitary. Without FSH, no egg matures, so ovulation does not occur. Hormonal methods are highly effective (over 99%) but can cause side effects such as headaches, mood changes and blood clots (rare).

Non-hormonal methods include: condoms (barrier method — prevent sperm reaching the egg and also protect against sexually transmitted infections), diaphragms (barrier placed over the cervix), copper IUDs (intrauterine devices that create an environment hostile to sperm), and surgical sterilisation (permanent). Non-hormonal methods do not affect the hormonal cycle but vary in effectiveness.

The OCR spec expects you to evaluate both types — consider effectiveness, side effects, convenience, protection against STIs, and whether the method is reversible.

Fertility treatments use hormones to help people who have difficulty conceiving (B3.2f, Higher Tier). FSH and LH injections can stimulate ovulation in women whose pituitary gland does not produce enough of these hormones naturally. This is called ovulation induction.

IVF (in vitro fertilisation) involves giving FSH to stimulate the ovaries to produce multiple eggs, collecting the eggs surgically, fertilising them with sperm in a laboratory dish, allowing the embryos to develop for a few days, and then implanting one or two embryos into the uterus. IVF success rates are around 25–30% per cycle. It is expensive, physically and emotionally demanding, and raises ethical concerns about unused embryos. However, it has allowed millions of people to have children who otherwise could not.

Plants also use hormones to coordinate growth and development. Auxin is a key plant hormone produced in the tips of shoots and roots. It controls phototropism (growth towards light) and gravitropism (growth in response to gravity).

In phototropism, light causes auxin to move to the shaded side of the shoot. Higher auxin concentration on the shaded side causes cells there to elongate more, bending the shoot towards the light. In gravitropism, auxin accumulates on the lower side of a horizontal root, where it inhibits cell elongation (the opposite effect to shoots), causing the root to grow downwards. In agriculture, synthetic auxins are used as selective weedkillers and rooting powders.

biology-paper-1.title: Homeostasis and Reproduction
biology-paper-1.description: Maintaining internal environments: blood glucose control, diabetes, and temperature regulation.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
What is Homeostasis?

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment (B3.3a). This is crucial because enzymes and other biological processes work best within narrow ranges of temperature, pH, water balance and blood glucose concentration. If internal conditions change too much, metabolic reactions slow down, become less efficient, or stop entirely — potentially killing the organism.

All homeostatic control systems have three key components working together: receptors (detect changes in the internal or external environment), a coordination centre (processes the information and determines the response — e.g. the brain, the pancreas or the thermoregulatory centre) and effectors (muscles or glands that bring about the corrective response). This system works through negative feedback — when a condition deviates from the normal level, the body acts to bring it back, then the response is switched off.

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains a stable internal environment using receptors, coordination centres and effectors working through negative feedback. It is essential for enzymes and metabolic reactions to function at their optimum rates.

Blood Glucose Control

Blood glucose concentration is monitored and controlled by the pancreas (B3.3b–c). When blood glucose rises (e.g. after eating a carbohydrate-rich meal), the pancreas detects the increase and secretes insulin. Insulin has two main effects: it causes body cells (especially muscle and liver cells) to take up glucose from the blood, and it stimulates the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen for storage. These actions lower the blood glucose back to normal.

When blood glucose drops (e.g. during exercise or between meals), the pancreas detects the decrease and secretes glucagon. Glucagon stimulates the liver to break stored glycogen back into glucose and release it into the blood, raising blood glucose back to normal. This opposing action of insulin and glucagon is a classic example of negative feedback — both hormones work together to keep blood glucose within a narrow, safe range.

Type 1 diabetes (B3.3d): The pancreas produces little or no insulin because the immune system has destroyed the insulin-producing beta cells (it is an autoimmune condition). Without insulin, blood glucose can rise to dangerously high levels after eating. Treatment requires regular insulin injections (or an insulin pump) combined with careful monitoring of blood glucose levels and carbohydrate intake. Type 1 usually develops in childhood or early adulthood and cannot be prevented.

Type 2 diabetes (B3.3d): The body’s cells become resistant to insulin — they no longer respond properly to it, even though the pancreas may still produce insulin (sometimes in reduced amounts). Blood glucose remains elevated because cells do not take up glucose effectively. Type 2 is strongly linked to obesity, a sedentary lifestyle, and genetic factors. Treatment involves a controlled diet (reducing sugar and refined carbohydrate intake), regular exercise, weight loss, and sometimes medication (such as metformin). In some cases, insulin injections may eventually be needed.

Type 2 diabetes is becoming increasingly common worldwide, particularly in countries with high obesity rates. It can often be prevented or managed through lifestyle changes, unlike Type 1 which cannot be prevented.

Key Fact

Type 1 diabetes: the pancreas does not produce insulin (autoimmune); treated with insulin injections. Type 2 diabetes: body cells become resistant to insulin (often lifestyle-linked, especially obesity); treated with diet, exercise and medication.

Temperature Regulation

Body temperature in humans is maintained at approximately 37°C by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain, which acts as the coordination centre. It receives information from temperature receptors in the skin (detecting external temperature) and in the blood (detecting core body temperature).

When the body is too hot, several effectors are activated: blood vessels near the skin surface vasodilate (widen), allowing more blood to flow close to the skin surface so more heat is lost to the surroundings by radiation. Sweat glands produce sweat that evaporates from the skin surface, transferring heat energy away from the body (evaporative cooling). Body hairs lie flat against the skin (reducing the insulating layer of trapped air).

When the body is too cold: blood vessels near the skin surface vasoconstrict (narrow), reducing blood flow near the surface and therefore reducing heat loss by radiation. Muscles shiver — rapid, involuntary contractions that generate heat from respiration in muscle cells. Body hairs stand up (erector muscles contract), trapping a thicker layer of insulating air close to the skin.

Temperature regulation is another example of negative feedback. If the body temperature rises above 37°C, cooling mechanisms activate to bring it down. If it drops below, warming mechanisms activate to bring it up. Once the temperature returns to normal, the response is switched off.

If temperature regulation fails, it can be life-threatening: hypothermia occurs when core body temperature drops below about 35°C (organs begin to fail), while heat stroke occurs when the body overheats and cannot cool down effectively (can cause organ damage).

biology-paper-2.title: Ecosystems
biology-paper-2.description: Biodiversity, food webs, trophic levels, and how biotic and abiotic factors affect communities.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Levels of Organisation in an Ecosystem

An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with each other and their physical environment (B4.1d). Ecosystems range in scale from a small pond to an entire ocean, but all share the same levels of organisation. Individual organisms of the same species living in the same area form a population. Different populations living together form a community. A community interacting with the abiotic (non-living) environment makes up the ecosystem.

Within communities, organisms depend on each other — this is interdependence (B4.1f). Key relationships include predation (one organism hunts and eats another), mutualism (both organisms benefit, such as bees pollinating flowers while collecting nectar) and parasitism (one organism benefits while the other is harmed, such as fleas on a dog). Organisms also compete for limited resources: animals compete for food, water, territory and mates, while plants compete for light, water, minerals and space.

Key Fact

Ecosystems are organised into: individual organisms → populations (one species) → communities (many species) → ecosystems (community + abiotic environment). Organisms are interdependent through predation, mutualism and parasitism.

Biotic and Abiotic Factors

Abiotic factors are non-living conditions that influence an ecosystem. Key examples include temperature, light intensity, moisture level, soil pH and wind speed. Biotic factors are living components: predators, prey availability, disease and competition between species (B4.1e). Changes in either type of factor affect the size and distribution of populations. For instance, a drought (abiotic) reduces plant growth, which in turn reduces herbivore populations (biotic knock-on effect).

Understanding these factors is essential for conservation. Scientists monitor abiotic factors like dissolved oxygen and pH in rivers to detect pollution, and track biotic indicators such as lichen diversity (which decreases with air pollution) or freshwater invertebrate species (some tolerate pollution, others do not).

An example of interdependence in action is the relationship between flowering plants and pollinating insects. Bees depend on flowers for nectar, and plants depend on bees for pollination. If one population declines — as seen with recent declines in bee numbers — the other is directly affected. This illustrates how changes in one part of an ecosystem ripple through the whole community.

The concept of niche is also important: every species has a specific role within its ecosystem, including what it eats, where it lives and how it interacts with other species. No two species can occupy exactly the same niche in the same area for long — one will outcompete the other. This is known as the competitive exclusion principle.

Pyramids of biomass represent the mass of organisms at each trophic level in a food chain. They are almost always pyramid-shaped (wider at the base) because energy is lost at each level. In contrast, pyramids of numbers can be inverted — for example, a single oak tree (one producer) may support thousands of insects. This is why biomass pyramids give a more accurate picture of energy flow than number pyramids.

Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight, captured by producers (green plants and algae) through photosynthesis. Energy then passes through trophic levels: producer → primary consumer (herbivore) → secondary consumer (carnivore) → tertiary consumer (top predator).

At each trophic level, energy is lost to the surroundings through respiration, movement and heat. This means less energy — and therefore less biomass — is available at each successive level. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels.

A food web shows all the interconnected food chains in a community. Removing or adding a species in a food web has knock-on effects throughout the community. For example, if a secondary consumer is removed, its prey population may increase rapidly, which then over-consumes the trophic level below.

Key Fact

Energy flows through trophic levels: producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer. Energy is lost at each level through respiration and heat, so biomass decreases up the chain.

Organisms have adaptations — inherited features that help them survive in their environment. These can be structural (e.g. thick fur for insulation in cold climates, or streamlined bodies for swimming), behavioural (e.g. migration to warmer areas in winter, or nocturnal hunting to avoid predators) or functional (e.g. producing venom to subdue prey, or antifreeze proteins in Arctic fish). Adaptations arise through natural selection over many generations.

Biodiversity refers to the variety of species in an ecosystem. High biodiversity makes an ecosystem more stable and resilient because if one species declines, others can fill its role. Human activities such as deforestation, pollution and over-hunting reduce biodiversity. Conservation programmes — including habitat protection, breeding programmes and seed banks — aim to maintain biodiversity for future generations.

Key Fact

Adaptations can be structural, behavioural or functional. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable. Conservation programmes protect endangered species and habitats.

biology-paper-2.title: Cycling Materials and Decomposition
biology-paper-2.description: How carbon and water cycle through ecosystems, and the vital role of decomposers.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
The Carbon Cycle

Many materials cycle through the abiotic and biotic components of an ecosystem (B4.1a). The carbon cycle is one of the most important. Carbon enters living organisms when plants absorb CO\(_2\) during photosynthesis. It passes through food chains when animals eat plants. Carbon is returned to the atmosphere through respiration (by all living organisms), combustion of fossil fuels and wood, and decomposition of dead organisms (B4.1c).

Over millions of years, some carbon becomes locked in fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and sedimentary rocks like limestone. Burning fossil fuels releases this stored carbon rapidly, increasing atmospheric CO\(_2\) concentrations. The oceans also act as a carbon sink, dissolving CO\(_2\) from the atmosphere, but rising levels are causing ocean acidification, which threatens marine life such as coral reefs and shellfish.

Key Fact

Carbon enters living organisms via photosynthesis and is returned to the atmosphere by respiration, combustion and decomposition. Only photosynthesis removes CO\(_2\) from the atmosphere. Fossil fuels lock carbon away for millions of years until combustion releases it.

The Water Cycle

The water cycle describes how water moves continuously between the Earth’s surface and atmosphere. Water evaporates from oceans, lakes and rivers (heated by the Sun), forming water vapour. Plants also release water vapour through transpiration from their leaves. As water vapour rises, it cools and condenses into clouds. Water returns to the ground as precipitation (rain, snow, hail) and is collected in rivers, lakes and underground stores before the cycle repeats.

The water cycle is essential because it provides fresh water for drinking, agriculture and industry. It also transports dissolved minerals through the soil, making nutrients available to plant roots. Human activities such as deforestation reduce transpiration, which can alter local rainfall patterns.

The nitrogen cycle is another critical nutrient cycle. Nitrogen gas (\(N_2\)) makes up 78% of the atmosphere but plants cannot use it directly. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil and in root nodules of legumes (peas, beans, clover) convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia (\(NH_3\)) and then into nitrates (\(NO_3^-\)), which plants absorb through their roots for making proteins and DNA. When organisms die, decomposers break down the nitrogen-containing compounds, and denitrifying bacteria convert some nitrates back into nitrogen gas, completing the cycle.

Understanding nutrient cycles is essential for sustainable agriculture. Farmers who grow legumes in rotation add nitrogen to the soil naturally, reducing the need for synthetic fertilisers. This mirrors how natural ecosystems recycle nutrients without human intervention.

Human activities disrupt these cycles. Burning fossil fuels increases atmospheric carbon faster than photosynthesis can remove it. Excessive use of nitrogen fertilisers leads to nutrient run-off into waterways, causing eutrophication — algal blooms that block light and deplete oxygen, killing aquatic organisms. Understanding both cycles helps explain why sustainable land management is so important.

In laboratory experiments, you can investigate decomposition by measuring the rate of decay of milk using pH indicators (as bacteria decompose lactose, they produce lactic acid, lowering pH) or by monitoring the mass loss of a compost bag over several weeks. Controlled variables include temperature, moisture and initial mass. These experiments demonstrate the real-world principles of nutrient recycling in a measurable, quantitative way.

Decomposition is the breakdown of dead organic matter by bacteria and fungi (known as decomposers). These microorganisms secrete enzymes onto dead material, digest it externally, and absorb the soluble products. Decomposition releases CO\(_2\) back into the atmosphere through the decomposers’ respiration and returns essential minerals (such as nitrates, phosphates and potassium) to the soil, where they can be taken up by plant roots.

Without decomposition, dead organisms and waste would accumulate, and the nutrients locked within them would never be recycled. This would eventually starve living plants of the minerals they need for growth.

Key Fact

Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead matter, recycling carbon and minerals back into the ecosystem. Without decomposition, nutrients would remain locked in dead organisms.

The rate of decomposition depends on several factors (B4.2b). Temperature — warm conditions increase enzyme activity in decomposers, but very high temperatures denature the enzymes. Moisture — water is needed for chemical reactions and for decomposers to survive. Oxygen — aerobic decomposers respire faster with more oxygen, breaking down material more quickly. Surface area — smaller pieces decompose faster because more surface is exposed to enzymes.

Composting applies these principles deliberately. Gardeners and farmers shred material (increases surface area), turn compost heaps regularly (introduces oxygen) and keep them moist and warm. The resulting compost is rich in minerals and can be used as a natural fertiliser, reducing the need for chemical alternatives.

In anaerobic conditions (without oxygen), decomposition still occurs but more slowly, and produces methane rather than CO\(_2\). This is why waterlogged landfill sites produce methane, a potent greenhouse gas.

Key Fact

Decomposition is fastest in warm, moist, oxygen-rich conditions with high surface area. Composting uses these principles to recycle organic waste into nutrient-rich soil.

biology-paper-2.title: Inheritance
biology-paper-2.description: Genes, alleles, genotypes, phenotypes and Punnett square crosses for single gene inheritance.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Genes, Chromosomes and DNA

The genome is the entire set of genetic material in an organism. In humans, DNA is packaged into 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total) inside the nucleus of most cells. Each chromosome carries hundreds of genes — short sections of DNA that code for specific proteins. These proteins determine our characteristics, from eye colour to blood type (B5.1a).

Most body cells are diploid — they contain two copies of each chromosome (one from each parent). Sex cells (gametes) are haploid, containing just one set of 23 chromosomes. At fertilisation, two haploid gametes fuse to restore the diploid number (B5.1b).

Key Fact

Human body cells are diploid (46 chromosomes in 23 pairs). Gametes are haploid (23 chromosomes). At fertilisation, two gametes fuse to restore the diploid number.

Alleles and Inheritance

Because chromosomes come in pairs, we have two copies of each gene — one from each parent. Different versions of a gene are called alleles. If both alleles are the same, the individual is homozygous (e.g. BB or bb). If the alleles are different, the individual is heterozygous (e.g. Bb). A dominant allele is expressed whenever it is present (shown with a capital letter), while a recessive allele is only expressed when homozygous (both copies the same, shown with a lowercase letter) (B5.1c).

The combination of alleles an organism has is its genotype (e.g. Bb). The observable characteristic that results is the phenotype (e.g. brown eyes). The phenotype depends on both the genotype and environmental factors.

Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene (monogenic inheritance), such as ear lobe attachment or tongue rolling. However, most characteristics are influenced by multiple genes (polygenic inheritance), such as height, skin colour and intelligence. Polygenic traits show continuous variation — a range of phenotypes rather than distinct categories — and are strongly influenced by environmental factors alongside genetics.

The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, mapped the entire human genome — around 20,000–25,000 genes. This has enabled scientists to identify genes linked to inherited disorders, develop genetic tests, and research personalised medicine where treatments are tailored to a patient’s specific genetic makeup.

Genetic screening can identify carriers of conditions like cystic fibrosis before they have children, allowing informed family planning. Embryos created through IVF can be tested for genetic disorders using pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD), though this raises ethical questions about selecting embryos.

Meiosis is the type of cell division that produces gametes. During meiosis, chromosomes are shuffled and randomly assorted, and sections of DNA can be exchanged between chromosomes (crossing over). This creates genetically unique gametes, which is why siblings (other than identical twins) are genetically different from each other despite having the same parents. Meiosis is essential for maintaining genetic diversity within a population.

A Punnett square is used to predict the possible offspring from a genetic cross. Place one parent’s alleles along the top and the other parent’s alleles down the side. Each box shows a possible genotype of the offspring.

Example: crossing two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb) for a trait where B (brown eyes) is dominant over b (blue eyes):

The predicted ratio is 3 brown : 1 blue (genotype ratio 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb). This gives a 75% probability of the dominant phenotype and 25% probability of the recessive phenotype. Remember, these are probabilities — actual results may differ due to chance, especially with small sample sizes.

For OCR Gateway, you should be able to construct genetic diagrams showing: parental phenotypes and genotypes, gametes, a Punnett square, and offspring ratios with probabilities (B5.1d).

Key Fact

A Punnett square predicts offspring genotypes and phenotypes. Crossing Bb × Bb gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio (75% dominant, 25% recessive). These are probabilities, not certainties.

Some genetic disorders are caused by faulty alleles. Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (ff). A person must be homozygous recessive to have the condition; heterozygous individuals (Ff) are carriers — they carry the allele but do not show symptoms. If two carriers have children, there is a 25% chance each child will have cystic fibrosis.

Polydactyly (extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele (D). Only one copy of the allele is needed for the condition to appear, so a cross between Dd and dd gives a 50% chance of affected offspring.

Sex is determined by the 23rd chromosome pair. Females have XX, males have XY. Since the father can pass either an X or a Y chromosome, there is a 50:50 chance of a child being male or female (B5.1e).

Key Fact

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (two copies needed). Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele (one copy is enough). Sex determination: XX = female, XY = male.

biology-paper-2.title: Natural Selection and Evolution
biology-paper-2.description: How variation, mutation and natural selection drive evolution and speciation.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Variation

Individuals within a species are not identical — they show variation. Some variation is genetic (caused by different alleles, e.g. blood type), some is environmental (caused by living conditions, e.g. a scar), and much is a combination of both (e.g. height is influenced by genes but also by diet). Genetic variation arises through mutations (random changes in DNA), meiosis (shuffling of chromosomes during gamete formation) and sexual reproduction (combining alleles from two parents) (B5.2a).

Variation within a population is essential for natural selection because it provides a range of characteristics on which selection can act. Without variation, all individuals would be equally suited (or unsuited) to their environment.

Key Fact

Variation can be genetic, environmental or both. Genetic variation comes from mutations, meiosis and sexual reproduction. Variation is essential for natural selection to occur.

Darwin’s Theory of Natural Selection

Charles Darwin proposed that species evolve through natural selection (B5.2b). The theory works in four steps:

1. Within a population, individuals show variation in their characteristics.
2. Individuals compete for limited resources such as food, water and mates.
3. Those with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce — this is ‘survival of the fittest’.
4. The advantageous alleles are passed to offspring, so over many generations the proportion of individuals with the beneficial trait increases.

Speciation occurs when populations of the same species become geographically or reproductively isolated. Over time, different environmental pressures and random mutations cause the two groups to evolve differently. Eventually, they become so genetically different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring — they are now separate species (B5.2c).

Extinction occurs when a species cannot adapt quickly enough to environmental changes. Causes include climate change, new predators or competitors, new diseases, habitat destruction and catastrophic events (e.g. volcanic eruptions, asteroid impacts). The fossil record provides evidence of past extinctions and shows that the vast majority of species that have ever lived are now extinct.

Key Fact

Natural selection: variation → competition → survival of the fittest → advantageous alleles passed on. Over many generations, this changes species — this is evolution.

Evidence for Evolution

Key evidence for evolution includes the fossil record (showing gradual changes in organisms over millions of years), comparative anatomy (similar bone structures in different species, suggesting common ancestry) and DNA analysis (closely related species share more DNA sequences). Darwin’s observations of finch beak shapes on the Galápagos Islands remain a classic example of natural selection in action (B5.2d).

Another well-known example is the peppered moth during the Industrial Revolution. Before industrialisation, light-coloured moths were well camouflaged on pale, lichen-covered trees. Dark (melanic) moths were rare because they were easily spotted by predators. As pollution killed lichens and darkened tree bark with soot, dark moths gained the advantage — they were better camouflaged and survived in greater numbers. When the Clean Air Acts reduced pollution, the light form became dominant again. This demonstrates natural selection responding to environmental change within observable timescales.

The theory of evolution by natural selection was independently proposed by both Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace in the mid-19th century. While Darwin is more famous, Wallace reached similar conclusions from his own fieldwork in Southeast Asia. Their joint paper was presented to the Linnean Society in 1858.

Darwin’s theory was controversial at the time because it contradicted the prevailing religious belief in creation. Today, the evidence from fossils, DNA, comparative anatomy and observed examples (such as antibiotic resistance) makes evolution one of the most strongly supported theories in biology.

It is important to note that individual organisms do not evolve — populations evolve over many generations as the frequency of advantageous alleles increases. Evolution has no direction or goal; it simply reflects which traits happen to be best suited to the current environment. A trait that is advantageous in one environment may become disadvantageous if conditions change.

Antibiotic resistance is a modern example of natural selection. When a population of bacteria is exposed to an antibiotic, most die. However, random mutations may have given some bacteria resistance. These resistant individuals survive, reproduce rapidly and pass on the resistance allele. Over time, the resistant strain becomes dominant (B5.2e).

MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a well-known resistant strain. To slow resistance, doctors should only prescribe antibiotics when necessary, and patients must complete the full course. Overuse in farming also contributes to the problem.

Key Fact

Antibiotic resistance is natural selection in bacteria: random mutation gives resistance, the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria, resistant ones survive and reproduce. Overuse of antibiotics speeds up this process.

Selective Breeding

Selective breeding (artificial selection) is when humans choose organisms with desirable traits and breed them together over many generations. Examples include breeding cows that produce more milk, wheat varieties resistant to disease, and dogs with specific temperaments. While selective breeding achieves rapid change, it reduces genetic variation within a population, which can make the population vulnerable to disease (B5.2f).

biology-paper-2.title: Monitoring and Maintaining the Environment
biology-paper-2.description: Sampling techniques, biodiversity measurement, and human impacts on ecosystems.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Monitoring Ecosystems

To understand the health of an ecosystem, scientists monitor the distribution and abundance of organisms (B6.1a). Field investigations use a range of sampling techniques to estimate population sizes without counting every individual.

Random sampling uses quadrats placed at random coordinates to avoid bias. Transect sampling places quadrats along a line to measure how distribution changes across a habitat (e.g. from woodland to open field). The capture-recapture method estimates animal populations: a sample is caught, marked, released, then a second sample is caught and the proportion of marked individuals is used to estimate total population size using the formula:

$$\text{Estimated population} = \frac{\text{number in 1st sample} \times \text{number in 2nd sample}}{\text{number marked in 2nd sample}}$$

Other equipment includes pooters (for small invertebrates), sweep nets, pitfall traps and identification keys.

The reliability of sampling depends on sample size and method. Random sampling avoids bias because the researcher does not choose where to place quadrats. In transect sampling, the regular spacing provides systematic data about how abiotic conditions (such as light or soil moisture) change across a habitat, and how this affects species distribution.

For capture-recapture to work accurately, several assumptions must hold: the marked individuals must have time to mix back into the population, marking must not affect survival or behaviour, and the population size must remain stable (no births, deaths, immigration or emigration) between samples. If these assumptions are violated, the estimate will be unreliable.

Another key technique is using quadrat grids with percentage cover estimates, where the researcher records what percentage of each quadrat is covered by a particular species. This is useful for plants and slow-moving organisms and gives more detail than simple presence/absence recording.

Environmental DNA (eDNA) is an emerging technique where scientists collect water or soil samples and analyse traces of DNA left behind by organisms. This allows them to detect the presence of elusive species without directly observing them — a non-invasive approach to monitoring biodiversity.

The OCR Gateway specification also requires understanding of eutrophication in detail. When excess nitrate or phosphate fertilisers wash into rivers and lakes, they stimulate rapid algal growth (algal bloom). The dense algae block sunlight, killing aquatic plants below the surface. When the algae die, decomposing bacteria multiply and consume dissolved oxygen. Oxygen levels fall so low that fish and other aerobic organisms suffocate. This sequence — nutrient enrichment, algal bloom, light blocking, decomposition, oxygen depletion — is a common exam question.

Conservation scientists use long-term monitoring data to track trends: is biodiversity increasing or decreasing? Are conservation measures working? Citizen science projects, where members of the public record sightings of species (e.g. the RSPB Big Garden Birdwatch), contribute millions of data points that scientists alone could never collect. This large-scale data helps identify declining species and target conservation efforts where they are needed most.

Key Fact

Sampling techniques include random quadrats (for plants), transects (to show change across a habitat) and capture-recapture (for mobile animals). Results are scaled up to estimate total population size (B6.1a).

Human Interactions with Ecosystems

Humans interact with ecosystems in both positive and negative ways (B6.1b). Negative impacts include:

• Deforestation — removes habitats, reduces biodiversity and releases stored carbon.
• Pollution — air pollution from burning fossil fuels (SO\(_2\), NO\(_x\)) causes acid rain; water pollution from fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication.
• Over-exploitation — overfishing and over-hunting reduce populations faster than they can recover.
• Introduction of invasive species — non-native species outcompete native organisms for resources.

Indicator species reveal pollution levels without expensive equipment (B6.1c). Lichens are indicators of air quality — bushy lichens grow only in clean air, while crusty lichens tolerate pollution. Freshwater invertebrates indicate water quality: stonefly larvae and freshwater shrimp need clean, oxygen-rich water; bloodworms and rat-tailed maggots tolerate polluted, low-oxygen water.

Scientists also use direct measurements: dissolved oxygen meters, pH probes and turbidity tubes provide quantitative data that can be compared over time or between sites. Combining biological and physical indicators gives a more complete picture of ecosystem health.

Key Fact

Indicator species show pollution levels: lichens for air quality, freshwater invertebrates for water quality. Their presence or absence provides evidence of environmental conditions.

Sustainability means using resources in a way that meets current needs without compromising future generations (B6.1d). Conservation strategies include:

• Protected areas — national parks and nature reserves limit human activity.
• Breeding programmes — captive breeding of endangered species with planned reintroduction to the wild.
• Seed banks — storing seeds from rare plant species as a safeguard against extinction.
• Fishing quotas and logging regulations — controlling how much is taken from ecosystems.
• Reforestation — planting trees to restore habitats and absorb CO\(_2\).

Effective conservation requires scientific monitoring to measure whether strategies are working, and cooperation between governments, scientists and local communities.

Key Fact

Sustainability means meeting present needs without harming future generations. Conservation uses protected areas, breeding programmes, seed banks, quotas and reforestation to maintain biodiversity.

biology-paper-2.title: Feeding the Human Race
biology-paper-2.description: Selective breeding, genetic engineering, and the challenge of food security.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
The Challenge of Food Security

The global human population is growing rapidly, creating increasing demand for food. Food security means having reliable access to sufficient, affordable, nutritious food. Achieving food security is one of the biggest global challenges biologists are helping to address (B6.2).

Threats to food security include: population growth (more people need more food), climate change (droughts and floods damage crops), rising costs (fuel and fertiliser prices increase food prices), conflict (war disrupts farming and food distribution) and water scarcity (irrigation becomes unreliable).

Key Fact

Food security is threatened by population growth, climate change, rising costs, conflict and water scarcity. Biologists develop solutions to increase food production sustainably.

Farming Techniques to Increase Yield

Farmers use various methods to increase the amount of food produced per area of land (yield):

• Fertilisers — provide essential minerals (nitrates for protein synthesis, phosphates for DNA and energy transfer, potassium for enzyme function). They can be organic (manure, compost) or inorganic (manufactured chemical fertilisers). Overuse of inorganic fertilisers can cause eutrophication in nearby waterways.
• Pesticides — kill organisms that damage crops: herbicides (kill weeds that compete with crops), insecticides (kill insect pests) and fungicides (kill fungal diseases). Pesticides increase yield but can harm non-target organisms and accumulate in food chains through bioaccumulation.

Biological control uses living organisms instead of chemicals to manage pests. Examples include introducing ladybirds to eat aphids, or using parasitic wasps that lay eggs inside caterpillars. Biological control avoids chemical pollution but can be unpredictable — the introduced organism may become an invasive species or fail to control the pest effectively (B6.2c).

Integrated pest management (IPM) combines chemical and biological methods, using pesticides only when necessary and relying on natural predators where possible. This reduces environmental damage while maintaining crop yields.

Key Fact

Biological control uses natural predators to manage pests, avoiding chemical pollution. However, introduced organisms can be unpredictable. IPM combines both approaches for best results.

Genetic Modification and Selective Breeding

Genetic modification (GM) involves inserting a gene from one organism into another to give it a new characteristic. GM crops can be engineered to be pest-resistant (reducing pesticide use), drought-tolerant (growing in dry conditions), or produce higher yields. For example, golden rice has been modified to produce beta-carotene (vitamin A), helping prevent blindness in developing countries (B6.2d).

Concerns about GM crops include: potential effects on wild populations if GM genes spread through cross-pollination, unknown long-term health effects, and ethical issues about ‘playing God’ with nature. Selective breeding (choosing organisms with desired traits and breeding them over many generations) is the traditional alternative but takes much longer and cannot introduce entirely new characteristics.

Sustainable farming aims to produce food without depleting resources or damaging the environment. Key practices include crop rotation (growing different crops each season to prevent soil mineral depletion and reduce pest build-up), organic farming (using natural fertilisers and biological control instead of chemicals), and reducing food miles (sourcing food locally to cut transport emissions).
