Hydroponics — growing plants in nutrient solutions without soil — allows year-round production in controlled environments, using less water and land than traditional farming. This is particularly useful in urban areas or regions with poor soil quality.

Another approach to food security is reducing food waste. Globally, roughly one-third of all food produced is wasted — either during production, distribution or by consumers. Improved storage, better supply chain management and public awareness campaigns can all help reduce waste and make existing food production go further.

Insect farming is also being explored as a sustainable protein source. Insects like crickets and mealworms require far less land, water and feed than traditional livestock. They produce fewer greenhouse gases and can be fed on organic waste. While not yet mainstream in Western diets, insects are already consumed by over 2 billion people worldwide.

The OCR Gateway specification also expects you to understand the concept of food miles — the distance food travels from producer to consumer. Shorter food miles mean less transport emissions. However, the picture is complex: food grown locally in heated greenhouses may have a larger carbon footprint than food imported from a country where it grows naturally outdoors. A full carbon footprint analysis considers energy use at every stage, not just transport.

The balance between increasing food production and protecting the environment is central to this topic. Intensive farming maximises yield but often damages ecosystems through pollution, habitat loss and soil degradation. Agroforestry (integrating trees with crops) and permaculture (designing farming systems that mimic natural ecosystems) offer alternative approaches that aim to produce food while supporting biodiversity and maintaining soil health for future generations.

Key Fact

GM crops can be pest-resistant, drought-tolerant or more nutritious, but concerns exist about gene transfer to wild plants and unknown long-term effects. Sustainable practices include crop rotation, organic farming and hydroponics.

biology-paper-2.title: Health, Disease and the Immune System
biology-paper-2.description: Communicable diseases, pathogens, the immune system and vaccination.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Health and Disease

Health is a state of physical and mental well-being, not just the absence of disease (B6.3a). Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens — microorganisms that infect and cause illness. Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. Communicable diseases can be spread by direct contact, airborne droplets, contaminated water or food, and animal vectors such as mosquitoes.

Non-communicable diseases cannot be spread between people. Examples include cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and asthma. Risk factors for non-communicable diseases include smoking, poor diet, lack of exercise, obesity and excessive alcohol consumption. Some non-communicable diseases have genetic components too.

Key Fact

Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists) and can spread between organisms. Non-communicable diseases (cancer, CVD, diabetes) cannot be passed on and are linked to lifestyle risk factors.

The Body’s Defence Systems

The body has several lines of defence against pathogens (B6.3b):

Non-specific defences (first line) prevent pathogens from entering the body. These include: skin (a physical barrier), mucus in the nose and airways (traps pathogens), cilia (tiny hairs that sweep mucus out of the airways), stomach acid (pH 1-2, kills most pathogens in food), and tears and saliva (contain the enzyme lysozyme, which breaks down bacterial cell walls).

If pathogens breach the first line, the body’s second line of defence — the inflammatory response — is activated. Damaged cells release chemicals that cause blood vessels to dilate and become more permeable. This increases blood flow to the area (causing redness and swelling) and allows white blood cells to reach the site of infection more quickly.

The different types of pathogen cause illness in different ways. Bacteria reproduce rapidly in the body and produce toxins that damage cells and tissues. Viruses are much smaller — they invade host cells, take over the cell’s machinery to replicate themselves, and burst out of the cell (lysis), destroying it in the process. Fungi can cause surface infections (e.g. athlete’s foot) or systemic infections in immunocompromised patients. Protists include the Plasmodium parasite that causes malaria, transmitted by mosquito vectors.

The interplay between communicable and non-communicable diseases is significant. For example, a weakened immune system (from HIV, a communicable disease) increases susceptibility to infections and certain cancers (non-communicable). Poor nutrition (a risk factor for non-communicable diseases) also weakens the immune system, making individuals more vulnerable to infections.

OCR Gateway also requires knowledge of specific diseases and how they spread. Salmonella is a bacterial disease spread through contaminated food. HIV is a virus spread through body fluids (blood, semen). Cholera is a bacterial disease spread through contaminated water. Understanding transmission routes helps develop prevention strategies such as vaccination, hygiene practices and vector control programmes.

Drug development follows a rigorous process. New medicines are first tested on cells and tissues in the lab (preclinical testing), then on animals to check for toxicity, before clinical trials on human volunteers. Phase 1 tests safety on healthy volunteers, Phase 2 tests effectiveness on patients, and Phase 3 involves larger groups with double-blind placebo controls. Only after passing all phases and regulatory review can a drug be approved for widespread use.

If pathogens get past the non-specific defences, lymphocytes mount a specific immune response. Each pathogen has unique proteins on its surface called antigens. Lymphocytes recognise these foreign antigens and produce antibodies — Y-shaped proteins that bind to the specific antigen, marking the pathogen for destruction.

Antibodies work by: clumping pathogens together (agglutination) so phagocytes can engulf them more easily, neutralising toxins produced by pathogens, and marking pathogens for destruction by other immune cells. After infection, some lymphocytes become memory cells that remain in the body for years. If the same pathogen enters again, memory cells produce antibodies much faster, often preventing illness entirely.

Phagocytes are white blood cells that carry out phagocytosis — they engulf and digest pathogens. This is a non-specific response (phagocytes attack any foreign cell).

Key Fact

Lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to antigens on pathogens. After infection, memory cells allow a faster response to reinfection. Phagocytes provide non-specific defence by engulfing pathogens.

Vaccination introduces a dead or weakened form of a pathogen (or its antigens) into the body. The immune system responds by producing antibodies and memory cells, without causing the disease. If the real pathogen enters later, memory cells trigger a rapid immune response. Vaccination programmes have eradicated smallpox and greatly reduced diseases like measles, polio and tetanus (B6.3c).

Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them reproducing. They work by targeting bacterial structures (e.g. cell walls) that human cells lack. Antibiotics do not work against viruses because viruses reproduce inside human cells and lack the structures antibiotics target. Overuse and misuse of antibiotics drives antibiotic resistance, creating ‘superbugs’ like MRSA (B6.3d).

Painkillers (e.g. paracetamol, ibuprofen) treat symptoms but do not kill pathogens. They relieve pain and reduce fever while the immune system fights the infection.

Key Fact

Vaccines introduce weakened pathogens to produce memory cells without causing disease. Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses. Overuse drives antibiotic resistance.

biology-paper-2.title: Non-Communicable Disease and Lifestyle
biology-paper-2.description: Cancer, cardiovascular disease, lifestyle factors and stem cell treatments.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Non-Communicable Diseases

Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) cannot be passed from one person to another (B6.3b). Unlike communicable diseases caused by pathogens, NCDs are caused by the interaction of multiple factors including genetics, lifestyle and environment (B6.3l). Major NCDs include cardiovascular diseases (heart disease and stroke), many forms of cancer, lung diseases (such as bronchitis), liver diseases (such as cirrhosis), and type 2 diabetes.

Non-communicable diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide. Understanding the risk factors that contribute to these diseases is essential for prevention and public health.

Lifestyle Risk Factors

The OCR Gateway specification requires you to analyse the effect of lifestyle factors on the incidence of NCDs at local, national and global levels (B6.3n). The key lifestyle factors are:

Smoking — damages the lining of arteries, leading to atherosclerosis (fatty deposits). Increases risk of cardiovascular disease, lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and bronchitis. Tar in cigarette smoke is a carcinogen — a cancer-causing substance.

Diet — a high-fat, high-salt, high-sugar diet increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and obesity. Too much saturated fat raises cholesterol levels, which contributes to atherosclerosis.

Alcohol — excessive alcohol consumption damages the liver, leading to cirrhosis (scarring of liver tissue). It also increases the risk of liver cancer and cardiovascular disease.

Lack of exercise — physical inactivity increases the risk of obesity, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Regular exercise helps maintain a healthy weight and strengthens the heart.

Key Fact

Key lifestyle risk factors for NCDs include smoking (cardiovascular disease, lung cancer), poor diet (CVD, type 2 diabetes), excessive alcohol (liver disease), and lack of exercise (obesity, CVD) (B6.3n).

Cardiovascular Disease

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death globally. It occurs when fatty deposits (atherosclerosis) build up inside coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. This can cause angina (chest pain) or, if the artery becomes completely blocked, a heart attack. A stroke occurs when blood supply to the brain is interrupted.

The spec requires you to evaluate different treatments for CVD (B6.3m). These include:

Lifestyle changes — improving diet, exercising more, stopping smoking, reducing alcohol. Low risk, but requires long-term commitment from the patient.

Medical treatments — statins lower blood cholesterol levels, reducing atherosclerosis. Blood thinners (anticoagulants/antiplatelets) reduce the risk of blood clots. Medication is effective but may have side effects.

Surgical treatments — stents are small tubes inserted into narrowed arteries to hold them open, restoring blood flow. Bypass surgery uses a blood vessel from another part of the body to create a new route for blood around the blocked artery. Surgery is effective but carries risks of infection and complications.

Key Fact

CVD treatments range from lifestyle changes (low risk, requires commitment) to medication (statins, blood thinners) to surgery (stents, bypass). Each has benefits and risks that must be evaluated (B6.3m).

Cancer

Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division (B6.3o). Mutations in the DNA that controls the cell cycle cause cells to divide rapidly, forming a tumour. Benign tumours do not spread to other parts of the body. Malignant tumours invade surrounding tissues and can spread to other organs through the blood — this is called metastasis.

Risk factors for cancer include smoking (lung cancer), UV radiation (skin cancer), certain viruses (e.g. HPV and cervical cancer), and genetic predisposition. Not all cancers have known causes.

When analysing data on lifestyle and disease, it is crucial to distinguish between correlation and causation. A correlation means two factors are linked (e.g. countries with higher smoking rates also have higher lung cancer rates). Causation means one factor directly causes the other. Correlation does not always mean causation — other variables (confounding factors) may be involved. Causation is only established through controlled experiments.

Stem cells have potential benefits in medicine (B6.3p). They can divide and differentiate into specialised cell types, so they could be used to replace damaged tissues. However, there are risks (e.g. tissue rejection after transplantation) and ethical concerns about using embryonic stem cells. The spec also asks about gene technology in medicine (B6.3q) and the importance of understanding the human genome for predicting disease likelihood and targeting treatments (B6.3r).

Key Fact

Correlation means two variables are linked; causation means one directly causes the other. Proving causation requires controlled experiments. Many NCD studies show correlations, not proof of causation.

chemistry-paper-1.title: The Particle Model
chemistry-paper-1.description: States of matter, particle arrangements, and the limitations of the particle model.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
States of Matter

All matter exists in one of three states of matter: solid, liquid and gas. The particle model explains the differences between these states by describing how particles are arranged, how they move, and how strongly they are held together.

In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction. They vibrate about these fixed positions but cannot move from place to place. This is why solids have a definite shape and a fixed volume. In a liquid, particles are close together but can move past each other. The forces of attraction are weaker than in a solid, giving liquids a fixed volume but no definite shape — they flow to fill the bottom of a container. In a gas, particles are far apart and move quickly in random directions. The forces of attraction are very weak, so gases have no fixed shape or volume and will spread out to fill any container.

Key Fact

Solids — particles in a regular arrangement, vibrate in fixed positions, close together. Liquids — particles close together but irregularly arranged, can slide past each other. Gases — particles far apart, move randomly at high speed.

Changes of State

When a substance is heated or cooled, it can change from one state to another. These are called changes of state. During a change of state, the particles themselves do not change — only the arrangement and movement of the particles change. This makes changes of state physical changes, not chemical changes, because they are reversible and no new substances are formed.

Melting — solid to liquid. Particles gain energy and overcome some of the forces holding them in fixed positions, so they can slide past each other. Boiling (or evaporation) — liquid to gas. Particles gain enough energy to overcome the remaining forces of attraction and escape into the air. Condensing — gas to liquid. Particles lose energy, slow down, and forces of attraction pull them closer together. Freezing — liquid to solid. Particles lose energy and lock into fixed positions. Sublimation — solid directly to gas without becoming a liquid first. Deposition — gas directly to solid.

During melting and boiling, energy is absorbed from the surroundings to break the forces between particles. During condensing and freezing, energy is released to the surroundings as new forces form between particles. Importantly, the temperature stays constant during a change of state — all the energy goes into breaking or forming intermolecular forces, not raising the temperature.

Key Fact

During a change of state, the temperature remains constant because the energy supplied is used to break (or form) forces between particles rather than increasing kinetic energy.

Heating and Cooling Curves

A heating curve is a graph of temperature against time for a substance being heated steadily. It shows: a rising section as the solid heats up, a flat section at the melting point (solid turning to liquid), a rising section as the liquid heats up, and a flat section at the boiling point (liquid turning to gas). The flat sections show that the substance is changing state — energy is being used to break intermolecular forces rather than raising the temperature.

A cooling curve shows the reverse process. The flat sections now represent condensation and freezing. A pure substance has sharp, flat plateaux at precise temperatures, while an impure substance changes state over a range of temperatures.

Physical Changes vs Chemical Changes

A physical change (such as a change of state) does not produce any new substances. The particles themselves stay the same — only their arrangement, spacing and energy change. Physical changes are reversible: ice can melt to water and then freeze back to ice. A chemical change forms new substances with different properties. Atoms are rearranged into new combinations. Chemical changes are usually irreversible under normal conditions — for example, burning magnesium in air produces magnesium oxide, which cannot easily be turned back into magnesium and oxygen.

The simple particle model represents particles as inelastic solid spheres (like bowling balls). This is useful for explaining states of matter and changes of state, but it has important limitations. The model does not account for the forces of attraction between particles, which are what actually hold substances together. It does not show that different particles have different sizes and masses. It does not represent the space between particles accurately — for example, gas particles are much further apart than diagrams usually show. It also fails to explain why different materials have different melting and boiling points, because it treats all particles as identical spheres. To explain differences in properties, we need to consider that the particles themselves (atoms, ions, molecules) and the bonds or forces between them are different in different substances.

Key Fact

The simple particle model (inelastic spheres) does not account for: forces of attraction between particles, different particle sizes, or the actual spacing between particles. It cannot explain why different materials have different properties.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Atomic Structure
chemistry-paper-1.description: Atomic models from Dalton to Bohr, sub-atomic particles, isotopes and ions.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
The Structure of the Atom

An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist. Atoms are incredibly small — a typical atomic radius is about \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m. Each atom has a tiny, dense nucleus at its centre. The nucleus contains two types of subatomic particle: protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons orbit the nucleus in energy levels (shells) and carry a negative charge.

Key Fact

Relative charges and approximate relative masses: Proton — charge +1, mass 1. Neutron — charge 0, mass 1. Electron — charge −1, mass approximately \(\frac{1}{1836}\) (negligible). The nuclear radius is much smaller than the radius of the atom — most of the atom is empty space.

Atomic Number and Mass Number

The atomic number tells you the number of protons in the nucleus. It defines what element an atom is — all atoms of the same element have the same atomic number. In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the atom has no overall charge. The mass number is the total number of protons plus neutrons.

To calculate the number of neutrons:

$$\text{number of neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{atomic number}$$

For example, sodium (Na) has atomic number 11 and mass number 23, so it has \(23 - 11 = 12\) neutrons, 11 protons and 11 electrons.

Isotopes and Ions

Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. This means they have different mass numbers but identical chemical properties. For example, carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, while carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.

An ion is an atom that has gained or lost electrons. Losing electrons forms a positive ion (cation) because there are now more protons than electrons. Gaining electrons forms a negative ion (anion). The nucleus does not change when an ion forms — only the number of electrons changes.

Standard notation shows mass number (top left), atomic number (bottom left) and chemical symbol. For example, \(^{23}_{11}\text{Na}\) tells you sodium has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. For ions, the charge is shown as a superscript: \(\text{Na}^+\) has lost one electron, \(\text{Cl}^-\) has gained one electron.

The Development of the Atomic Model

Our understanding of the atom has changed over time as new experimental evidence emerged.

Early 1800s

Dalton’s Model

John Dalton proposed atoms were tiny, solid, indivisible spheres. He thought all atoms of the same element were identical.

1897

Thomson’s Plum Pudding Model

J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

1909–1911

Rutherford, Geiger & Marsden

They fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through (the atom is mostly empty space), but some deflected at large angles and a few bounced back. This disproved the plum pudding model. Rutherford proposed the nuclear model: a small, dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting around it.

1913

Bohr’s Model

Niels Bohr refined the model by placing electrons in fixed energy levels at specific distances from the nucleus, rather than orbiting randomly.

Key Fact

The alpha scattering experiment disproved the plum pudding model. Most alpha particles passed through (mostly empty space), some bounced back (small, dense, positive nucleus).

Electronic Configuration

Electrons occupy energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons. The second and third shells each hold a maximum of 8. Electrons fill the lowest available energy level first.

Find the element’s atomic number (= number of electrons in a neutral atom). Fill the first shell with up to 2, the second with up to 8, and the third with up to 8. For example: oxygen (8 electrons) is 2, 6. Sodium (11 electrons) is 2, 8, 1. Calcium (20 electrons) is 2, 8, 8, 2. The number of outer-shell electrons matches the group number for Groups 1–7, explaining why elements in the same group react similarly.

The electronic configuration determines how an element reacts. Group 1 elements have one outer electron and lose it easily. Group 7 elements have seven outer electrons and tend to gain one. Group 0 elements have full outer shells and are very unreactive.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Purity and Separating Mixtures
chemistry-paper-1.description: Chemical purity, melting points, filtration, distillation and chromatography.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Pure Substances in Chemistry

In everyday language, “pure” often means natural or uncontaminated. In chemistry, the meaning is very specific: a pure substance is one that contains only a single element or a single compound. For example, pure water contains only \(H_2O\) molecules and nothing else. Orange juice labelled “pure” in a supermarket is not pure in the chemical sense because it is a mixture of water, sugars, citric acid and many other compounds. This distinction between the everyday and scientific meanings of “pure” is frequently tested in the exam.

You can test whether a substance is pure by measuring its melting point. A pure substance has a sharp, precise melting point — it melts at one exact temperature. An impure substance (a mixture) melts over a range of temperatures, and its melting point is lower than expected. Similarly, a pure substance has a fixed boiling point, while an impure substance boils over a range.

Key Fact

In chemistry, a pure substance contains only one element or one compound. A pure substance melts and boils at a single sharp temperature. An impure substance melts over a range of temperatures.

Relative Formula Mass

The relative formula mass (\(M_r\)) of a compound is found by adding up the relative atomic masses (\(A_r\)) of all the atoms in its formula. For example, for water \(H_2O\): \(M_r = (2 \times 1) + 16 = 18\). For calcium carbonate \(CaCO_3\): \(M_r = 40 + 12 + (3 \times 16) = 100\).

You can also deduce the empirical formula of a compound from the relative numbers of atoms present or from a model or diagram. The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio — for example, glucose \(C_6H_{12}O_6\) has the empirical formula \(CH_2O\) because the ratio of C:H:O is 1:2:1. You may be asked to deduce the empirical formula from a model, a diagram, or data about the relative numbers of atoms present.

Formulations

Many useful materials are formulations — mixtures that have been carefully designed so that each component is present in a measured quantity to give the product specific properties. Examples include alloys (mixtures of metals), paints, medicines, cleaning products and fuels. An alloy such as steel is a formulation of iron with small amounts of carbon and sometimes other metals such as chromium (in stainless steel). Other examples include paints (pigments, binders, solvents in precise ratios), medicines (active ingredient mixed with fillers and flavourings), and even concrete (cement, sand, gravel, water).

Separation Techniques

Because the components of a mixture are not chemically bonded, they can be separated by physical methods. The choice of technique depends on the properties of the substances in the mixture.

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel — the liquid passes through (the filtrate) and the solid stays behind (the residue). Crystallisation separates a dissolved solid (solute) from a solution. The solution is heated gently to evaporate the solvent until crystals begin to form, then left to cool so that more crystals grow. This is used to produce pure, dry samples of salts.

Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution — for example, water from salt water. The solution is heated until the solvent evaporates, then the vapour is cooled and condensed back into a liquid in a separate container. Fractional distillation separates a mixture of liquids with different boiling points. The mixture is heated in a flask fitted with a fractionating column. The liquid with the lowest boiling point evaporates first, rises to the top of the column, and is collected. Each liquid is collected separately as the temperature rises.

Chromatography

Chromatography separates dissolved substances. It works because different substances have different affinities for a stationary phase (such as paper) and a mobile phase (such as a solvent). In paper chromatography, a spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil line near the bottom of chromatography paper. The paper is placed in a solvent, which rises up the paper carrying the dissolved substances with it. Substances that are more soluble in the mobile phase travel further up the paper.

Key Fact

The \(R_f\) value identifies a substance and is calculated as: $$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$$ Each substance has a unique \(R_f\) value for a given solvent and stationary phase. A pure substance produces a single spot; a mixture produces multiple spots.

Other chromatographic methods include thin layer chromatography (TLC), which uses a thin layer of silica or alumina on a glass plate as the stationary phase, and gas chromatography, which uses a gas as the mobile phase. Locating agents (such as UV light or ninhydrin spray) may be needed to make colourless spots visible on the chromatogram. Gas chromatography uses a gas as the mobile phase and can separate complex mixtures that would be impossible to analyse by paper chromatography alone.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Bonding
chemistry-paper-1.description: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, electron transfer and sharing, dot-and-cross diagrams.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Why Atoms Bond

Atoms are most stable when they have a full outer shell of electrons. Most atoms do not naturally have a full outer shell, so they bond with other atoms to achieve one. There are three main types of chemical bond: ionic bonding, covalent bonding and metallic bonding. All chemical bonds involve electrostatic forces — the attraction between positive and negative charges. The type of bond that forms depends on whether the atoms involved are metals or non-metals and how many electrons are in their outer shells.

Ionic Bonding

Ionic bonding occurs between metals and non-metals. The metal atom transfers one or more electrons to the non-metal atom. The metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positively charged ion (cation). The non-metal atom gains electrons and becomes a negatively charged ion (anion). The oppositely charged ions are then held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction — this is the ionic bond.

For example, in sodium chloride (NaCl): sodium (2, 8, 1) loses one electron to become \(\text{Na}^+\) (2, 8), and chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to become \(\text{Cl}^-\) (2, 8, 8). Both ions now have full outer shells, making them stable. In magnesium oxide (MgO), magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses two electrons to become \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), and oxygen (2, 6) gains two electrons to become \(\text{O}^{2-}\). In an ionic compound, billions of ions are arranged in a regular three-dimensional structure called a giant ionic lattice, where each ion is surrounded by oppositely charged ions in all directions.

Key Fact

In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred from metal to non-metal. The resulting ions have opposite charges and attract each other. Ionic compounds form giant ionic lattices.

Covalent Bonding

Covalent bonding occurs between non-metal atoms. Instead of transferring electrons, the atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Each shared pair of electrons is one covalent bond. By sharing, both atoms achieve full outer shells. A single shared pair is a single bond, two shared pairs form a double bond (e.g. \(O_2\)), and three shared pairs form a triple bond (e.g. \(N_2\)).

For example, in a molecule of water (\(H_2O\)), the oxygen atom shares one pair of electrons with each of two hydrogen atoms, forming two covalent bonds. In chlorine gas (\(Cl_2\)), two chlorine atoms each share one pair of electrons, forming a single covalent bond. Covalent compounds include small simple molecules (like \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\), \(CH_4\)) and enormous giant covalent structures (like diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide).

Dot-and-cross diagrams show how electrons are arranged in a bond. Use dots for the electrons from one atom and crosses for the electrons from the other. For ionic compounds, show the electron transfer and put each ion in square brackets with its charge. For covalent compounds, show the shared pairs in the overlap between the two atoms. These diagrams are a useful model but have limitations: they do not show the three-dimensional shape of molecules, the relative sizes of atoms, or the distances between atoms. Ball-and-stick models and space-filling models address some of these limitations but introduce others. No single model is perfect — each emphasises different aspects of bonding.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, the atoms are arranged in a regular structure. The outer-shell electrons are delocalised — they are free to move through the whole structure rather than being attached to individual atoms. This leaves behind a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a “sea” of delocalised electrons. The strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the negative delocalised electrons is what holds the metal together.

Types of Structure

Substances can have different types of structure, which affects their properties:

Giant ionic lattices (e.g. NaCl) — regular arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions, held by strong ionic bonds in all directions. Simple molecular structures (e.g. \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\)) — small molecules with strong covalent bonds within molecules but weak intermolecular forces between molecules. Giant covalent structures (e.g. diamond, graphite) — huge networks of atoms all bonded by strong covalent bonds. Polymers — very long chain molecules made of repeating units joined by covalent bonds. Metallic structures — regular lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.

Key Fact

Chemical bonding is always about electrostatic forces: ionic = attraction between opposite ions; covalent = shared electron pairs attracting both nuclei; metallic = positive ions attracted to delocalised electrons.

The Periodic Table helps predict bonding type. Elements on the left (metals) tend to lose electrons. Elements on the right (non-metals) tend to gain or share electrons. An element’s position in the table — its group and period — tells you its electronic configuration, which determines how it bonds. Group 1 elements have one outer electron and form +1 ions; Group 7 elements have seven outer electrons and gain one to form −1 ions. Elements in Group 0 have full outer shells and do not readily bond.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Properties of Materials
chemistry-paper-1.description: How bonding type determines physical properties of ionic, covalent and metallic substances.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Linking Structure to Properties

The physical properties of a substance — its melting point, boiling point, hardness and electrical conductivity — depend on its type of bonding and structure. Understanding this link is one of the most important ideas in chemistry: if you know the bonding, you can predict the properties. The exam frequently tests your ability to explain properties in terms of structure and bonding, so it is essential to link every property back to the forces involved.

Ionic Compounds

Ionic compounds such as sodium chloride have giant ionic lattice structures. They have high melting and boiling points because a large amount of energy is needed to break the many strong electrostatic forces between the ions. They do not conduct electricity when solid because the ions are held in fixed positions. However, they do conduct when molten or dissolved in water because the ions become free to move and carry charge. Ionic compounds are often brittle — when a force is applied, layers of ions shift and like charges line up, causing repulsion that shatters the crystal. Most ionic compounds are also soluble in water because water molecules can surround and separate the individual ions.

Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (strong ionic bonds), conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved (ions must be free to move), do not conduct as solids (ions fixed in place).

Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecular substances (such as water, carbon dioxide and oxygen) have strong covalent bonds within each molecule but weak intermolecular forces between molecules. It is these weak intermolecular forces that are overcome when the substance melts or boils — not the covalent bonds. This means simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points and are often gases or liquids at room temperature. They do not conduct electricity in any state because they have no free electrons or ions to carry charge. It is a very common exam error to say the covalent bonds are weak — the bonds within the molecules are strong; it is the forces between molecules that are weak.

Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces because there are more electrons that can create temporary dipoles. This means larger molecules tend to have higher boiling points. For example, the boiling point of methane (\(CH_4\), small molecule) is much lower than that of octane (\(C_8H_{18}\), larger molecule). The strength of the intermolecular forces depends on the size of the molecule, not the strength of the covalent bonds within it.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures contain billions of atoms all bonded by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network. They have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. Carbon has several giant covalent allotropes — different structural forms of the same element, each with distinct physical properties:

Carbon can form four covalent bonds. In diamond, each carbon atom bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral arrangement — making it extremely hard and unable to conduct electricity (no free electrons). In graphite, each carbon bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers with weak forces between layers, allowing them to slide over each other (making graphite soft and slippery). One electron per carbon atom is delocalised within each layer, so graphite does conduct electricity. Fullerenes (e.g. \(C_{60}\) buckminsterfullerene) are hollow carbon molecules shaped like balls or tubes. Graphene is a single layer of graphite — one atom thick, incredibly strong, an excellent electrical conductor, and a potential material for electronics and composites.

Key Fact

Carbon can form four covalent bonds. Diamond (4 bonds per C, very hard, non-conductor), Graphite (3 bonds per C, layers slide, conducts electricity), Graphene (single layer of graphite, strong, conducts), Fullerenes (hollow molecules, e.g. \(C_{60}\)).

Polymers and Metals

Polymers are very long chain molecules made of repeating units. They are held together by strong covalent bonds along the chain and weaker intermolecular forces between chains. Their properties depend on what the repeating unit is and how the chains are arranged. Metals have high melting points, conduct electricity (delocalised electrons), and are malleable (layers of positive ions can slide over each other without breaking the metallic bond, because the delocalised electrons can adjust to the new positions). Metals are also good conductors of heat because the delocalised electrons transfer kinetic energy quickly through the structure.

You can use data such as melting point and boiling point to predict the state of a substance at a given temperature. If the temperature is below the melting point, the substance is solid. Between melting and boiling point, it is liquid. Above the boiling point, it is a gas. For example, water (melting point 0°C, boiling point 100°C) is solid below 0°C, liquid between 0°C and 100°C, and gas above 100°C. This skill is commonly tested using data tables.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
chemistry-paper-1.description: Writing formulae, balancing equations, conservation of mass, and the mole concept.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Chemical Symbols and Formulae

Every element has a unique chemical symbol, shown on the periodic table. Compounds are represented by chemical formulae that show which elements are present and how many atoms of each. For example, \(H_2O\) tells you water contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. \(CaCO_3\) tells you calcium carbonate contains 1 calcium, 1 carbon and 3 oxygen atoms. Small subscript numbers apply to the element directly before them; a number before a formula (a coefficient) multiplies every atom in that formula.

Working out the formula of a compound from its name requires knowledge of ion charges. For example, sodium chloride is \(NaCl\) because \(Na^+\) and \(Cl^-\) balance in a 1:1 ratio. Magnesium oxide is \(MgO\) (\(Mg^{2+}\) and \(O^{2-}\)).

Key Fact

Chemical formulae show which elements are present and the ratio of atoms. Subscript numbers apply to the preceding element; coefficients multiply the whole formula. \(H_2O\) = 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen.

Writing and Balancing Equations

A chemical equation shows reactants on the left and products on the right, separated by an arrow (\(\rightarrow\)). A word equation uses names: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. A symbol equation uses formulae: \(2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO\).

Symbol equations must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides. This reflects the conservation of mass — atoms are rearranged in reactions but never created or destroyed (C3.1a). To balance an equation: count atoms on each side, add coefficients (large numbers in front of formulae) until both sides match, and never change the subscript numbers in a formula.

Balance the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water:

Unbalanced: \(H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow H_2O\)

Count atoms: Left — 2 H, 2 O. Right — 2 H, 1 O. Oxygen is unbalanced.

Put a 2 in front of \(H_2O\): \(H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\). Now right side has 4 H and 2 O. Left has 2 H and 2 O. Hydrogen is unbalanced.

Put a 2 in front of \(H_2\): \(2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\). Now both sides have 4 H and 2 O. Balanced.

Key Fact

Equations must be balanced: same number of atoms on each side. Add coefficients to balance — never change subscript numbers. Conservation of mass: total mass of reactants = total mass of products.

State Symbols

State symbols are written after each formula to show the physical state: (s) = solid, (l) = liquid, (g) = gas, (aq) = aqueous (dissolved in water). For example:

$$2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)$$

State symbols give extra information about reaction conditions and help you understand whether substances are dissolved, gaseous, etc.

Conservation of mass can be demonstrated experimentally. If you carry out a reaction in a sealed container and measure the total mass before and after, it remains the same. In open containers, reactions that produce gas may appear to lose mass (because the gas escapes), but the total mass of all products — including the gas — equals the total mass of reactants.

An important application of balanced equations is calculating reacting masses. Using relative atomic masses from the periodic table, you can work out how much product will form from a given amount of reactant. For example, from \(2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO\): 2 moles of magnesium (48 g) react with 1 mole of oxygen (32 g) to form 2 moles of magnesium oxide (80 g). This confirms conservation of mass: 48 + 32 = 80.

You should also be aware of the difference between exothermic reactions (which release energy to the surroundings, causing a temperature rise, e.g. combustion and neutralisation) and endothermic reactions (which absorb energy from the surroundings, causing a temperature drop, e.g. thermal decomposition and dissolving ammonium nitrate in water). Energy changes during reactions are linked to the breaking and forming of chemical bonds.

Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic process), while forming bonds releases energy (exothermic process). In an exothermic reaction, the energy released by forming new bonds exceeds the energy needed to break existing bonds, so the overall reaction releases energy to the surroundings and the temperature rises. In an endothermic reaction, the opposite is true — more energy is needed to break bonds than is released when new bonds form.

Types of Chemical Reaction

OCR Gateway requires knowledge of several reaction types (C3.1b):

• Combustion: a substance reacts with oxygen, releasing energy. \(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\)
• Displacement: a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one. \(Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu\)
• Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. \(HCl + NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
• Oxidation: gaining oxygen (or losing electrons). Reduction: losing oxygen (or gaining electrons). Redox reactions involve both.
• Thermal decomposition: a substance breaks down when heated. \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\)

Key Fact

Key reaction types: combustion (fuel + oxygen), displacement (reactive metal replaces less reactive one), neutralisation (acid + base → salt + water), thermal decomposition (breaks down with heat). All must be balanced.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Energetics
chemistry-paper-1.description: Exothermic and endothermic reactions, reaction profiles, activation energy and bond energies.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Energy Changes in Reactions

Every chemical reaction involves an energy change. Energy is either transferred to the surroundings or absorbed from them. The key principle is that energy is transferred, never created or destroyed. Two categories describe the direction of energy transfer. Understanding these categories — and the bond-level explanation for why energy is transferred — is fundamental to the whole of chemistry. Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between the system and the surroundings.

Key Fact

Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings increases. Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

Exothermic reactions include combustion (burning fuels), neutralisation (acid + alkali), and many oxidation reactions. Everyday examples include hand warmers (the crystallisation of a supersaturated sodium acetate solution) and self-heating food cans. Endothermic reactions include thermal decomposition, the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate, thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, and photosynthesis. Sports cold packs are a practical example — the endothermic dissolution of ammonium nitrate in water absorbs heat, cooling the injured area.

Measuring Energy Changes (PAG C5)

You can identify whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic by measuring the temperature change of the surroundings (usually a solution in a polystyrene cup). If the temperature rises, the reaction is exothermic. If the temperature falls, the reaction is endothermic. A polystyrene cup is used as an insulator to reduce heat loss to the surroundings, giving a more accurate temperature reading. You should record the starting temperature, the maximum (or minimum) temperature, and calculate the change. In a well-insulated system, a bigger temperature change indicates a more energetic reaction.

Reaction Profiles

A reaction profile is a diagram that shows the energy levels of the reactants and products, and the energy change during a reaction. On the vertical axis is energy; on the horizontal axis is the progress of the reaction (sometimes labelled “reaction pathway”). The diagram does not show time — it simply shows the energy changes as reactants transform into products.

For an exothermic reaction, the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants — the energy difference has been released to the surroundings. The profile shows a “hump” from reactants rising to a peak (the activation energy barrier) then falling to a lower product level. For an endothermic reaction, the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants — energy has been absorbed. The profile shows a hump rising to the peak then settling at a level higher than the starting point. In both cases, the hump represents the activation energy — the minimum energy needed for the reaction to start. You must label four things on any reaction profile: the energy level of reactants, the energy level of products, the activation energy (from reactants to the peak), and the overall energy change (from reactants to products).

Key Fact

Activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a reaction to occur. It is shown on a reaction profile as the difference between the reactant energy level and the top of the energy barrier (the peak).

Bond Energy Calculations (Higher)

During a chemical reaction, bonds in the reactants must be broken (this requires energy — endothermic) and new bonds in the products are made (this releases energy — exothermic). The overall energy change depends on the balance between these two processes. This is a Higher Tier calculation that requires you to use given bond energy values:

Step 1: Add up the total energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants. Step 2: Add up the total energy released when all the bonds in the products are formed. Step 3: Calculate the overall energy change:

$$\text{energy change} = \text{energy to break bonds} - \text{energy released making bonds}$$

If the answer is positive, the reaction is endothermic (more energy needed to break bonds than is released making them). If the answer is negative, the reaction is exothermic (more energy released making bonds than needed to break them).

For example, for \(H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2HCl\): breaking bonds = H–H (436 kJ) + Cl–Cl (242 kJ) = 678 kJ. Making bonds = 2 × H–Cl (431 kJ) = 862 kJ. Energy change = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ. Negative, so exothermic. More energy was released making the H–Cl bonds than was required to break the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds, so the surplus energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat. This is why the overall reaction is exothermic. Remember: you must always consider all bonds broken and all bonds made, not just some of them.

Key Fact

Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic). Making bonds releases energy (exothermic). If more energy is released making bonds than absorbed breaking them, the reaction is exothermic overall.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Types of Chemical Reactions and Electrolysis
chemistry-paper-1.description: Redox, acids, neutralisation, pH scale, and electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or the loss of electrons. Reduction is the loss of oxygen or the gain of electrons. These always happen together in what are called redox reactions. A useful mnemonic is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

For example, when copper oxide is reduced by carbon: \(2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2\). The copper oxide loses oxygen (it is reduced) and the carbon gains oxygen (it is oxidised). Carbon is the reducing agent (it causes the reduction of copper oxide) and copper oxide is the oxidising agent (it causes the oxidation of carbon). At Higher Tier, you also need to explain redox in terms of electrons: the substance that is oxidised loses electrons, and the substance that is reduced gains electrons. For example, in the formation of magnesium oxide: \(Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-\) (oxidation) and \(O + 2e^- \rightarrow O^{2-}\) (reduction).

Key Fact

Oxidation = gain of oxygen OR loss of electrons. Reduction = loss of oxygen OR gain of electrons. In terms of electrons (Higher): the substance that is oxidised loses electrons; the substance that is reduced gains electrons.

Acids and Alkalis

Acids produce hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)) when they dissolve in water. Solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)). The pH scale measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is, running from 0 (very strong acid) to 14 (very strong alkali). pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and above 7 is alkaline. Each step on the pH scale represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

You can measure pH using universal indicator (which changes colour across a range: red for strong acids, green for neutral, purple for strong alkalis) or a pH meter (which gives a precise numerical reading). Litmus paper gives a simple acid/alkali test but cannot distinguish between different strengths.

Dilute and concentrated refer to the amount of acid dissolved in a given volume of water. Strong and weak refer to the degree of ionisation. A strong acid (e.g. hydrochloric acid) fully ionises in water — every molecule produces \(H^+\) ions. A weak acid (e.g. ethanoic acid) only partially ionises — only some molecules produce \(H^+\) ions. When the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of ten, the pH decreases by one.

Neutralisation and Making Salts

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base or alkali to form a salt plus water. The ionic equation for neutralisation is:

$$H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)$$

Key reactions to know:

Acid + metal \(\rightarrow\) salt + hydrogen. For example: \(Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)\).

Acid + metal carbonate \(\rightarrow\) salt + water + carbon dioxide. For example: \(CaCO_3(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow CaCl_2(aq) + H_2O(l) + CO_2(g)\).

Acid + alkali \(\rightarrow\) salt + water. For example: \(NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)\).

Key Fact

The name of the salt depends on the acid used: hydrochloric acid \(\rightarrow\) chloride salts, sulfuric acid \(\rightarrow\) sulfate salts, nitric acid \(\rightarrow\) nitrate salts.

Electrolysis

Electrolysis is the process of using an electric current to decompose (break down) an ionic compound that is either molten or dissolved in water. The ionic compound must be in a liquid state (molten or dissolved in water) so that the ions are free to move and carry the electrical current. Solid ionic compounds cannot be electrolysed because their ions are held in fixed positions within the lattice.

The ionic compound is placed in a container with two electrodes connected to a power supply. Positive ions (cations) move towards the cathode (negative electrode), where they gain electrons and are reduced. Negative ions (anions) move towards the anode (positive electrode), where they lose electrons and are oxidised. Metals (or hydrogen) form at the cathode; non-metals form at the anode.

For molten binary compounds, predicting products is straightforward. For example, molten sodium chloride produces sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode. For aqueous solutions, there are competing reactions because water also contains \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions. At the cathode, hydrogen is produced instead of the metal if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen. At the anode, oxygen is usually produced (from \(OH^-\) ions) unless halide ions are present, in which case the halogen is produced. For example, electrolysing aqueous copper sulfate with inert (carbon) electrodes produces copper at the cathode (because copper is less reactive than hydrogen) and oxygen at the anode (because no halide ions are present). The electrodes used matter: inert electrodes (such as carbon or platinum) do not take part in the reaction, whereas non-inert electrodes (such as copper) can themselves dissolve or be deposited during electrolysis.

Key Fact

At the cathode: \(\text{Na}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Na}\) (reduction). At the anode: \(2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-\) (oxidation). Half equations show what happens at each electrode separately.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Predicting Chemical Reactions — Reactivity
chemistry-paper-2.description: Reactivity series, displacement reactions, and metal extraction using carbon.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity series. The most reactive metals (such as potassium and sodium) are at the top, and the least reactive (such as gold and platinum) are at the bottom. The reactivity of a metal depends on how easily it forms a positive ion by losing its outer-shell electrons. Metals higher in the series lose electrons more readily because their outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electron shells.

The order from most to least reactive is: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold, platinum. Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points even though they are not metals — carbon’s position determines how metals can be extracted, and hydrogen’s position determines which metals react with dilute acids.

Key Fact

A metal’s reactivity depends on how easily it loses its outer electrons to form a positive ion. More reactive metals react more vigorously with water and dilute acids. The tendency to form positive ions increases up the reactivity series.

Reactions of Metals

You can deduce the reactivity of a metal from its reactions with water and dilute acids. Very reactive metals (K, Na, Li, Ca) react vigorously with cold water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. For example, sodium reacts with water: \(2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)\). Calcium reacts more gently, producing a cloudy solution as calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble.

Moderately reactive metals (Mg, Zn, Fe) react very slowly or not at all with cold water but react well with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen gas. For example, magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: \(Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)\). Unreactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au) do not react with water or dilute acids because they do not lose their electrons easily enough.

Displacement Reactions

A displacement reaction occurs when a more reactive metal replaces a less reactive metal from a compound. For example, if you place iron in copper sulfate solution, the iron displaces the copper:

$$Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)$$

The iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it. The blue copper sulfate solution turns colourless (iron sulfate) and a brown coating of copper appears on the iron. A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one — copper in iron sulfate solution would show no reaction. This principle can be applied to any pair of metals: if the added metal is higher in the reactivity series than the metal in the salt, displacement occurs.

You can work out a reactivity order by doing a series of displacement experiments. Place different metals into solutions of other metal salts. If a displacement occurs (colour change, solid deposited, temperature rise), the added metal is more reactive. If nothing happens, the added metal is less reactive. By testing several combinations systematically, you can rank the metals in order of reactivity. You can also compare how vigorously different metals react with dilute acid — faster fizzing and more heat indicates higher reactivity.

Extracting Metals

How a metal is extracted from its ore depends on its position in the reactivity series. Metals below carbon in the series (such as iron, zinc and copper) can be extracted by reduction with carbon. The carbon is more reactive, so it displaces the metal from its oxide and takes the oxygen. For example, extracting iron from iron oxide:

$$2Fe_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Fe + 3CO_2$$

In this reaction, the iron oxide is reduced (loses oxygen) and the carbon is oxidised (gains oxygen). This is why carbon reduction is also a redox reaction. Metals above carbon in the series (such as aluminium, sodium and potassium) are too reactive to be extracted by carbon. They must be extracted by electrolysis, which is more expensive because it uses large amounts of electricity. For example, aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide (bauxite) by electrolysis at around 960°C.

Biological methods offer alternatives to traditional extraction, particularly for low-grade ores where conventional mining is not economically viable. Phytoextraction uses plants to absorb metal compounds from the soil through their roots; the plants are harvested and burned, and the metal is extracted from the ash. Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce acidic solutions that dissolve metal compounds from the ore; the metal can then be extracted from the solution by displacement or electrolysis. These methods are slower but have lower environmental impact and can extract metals from ores that would otherwise be waste.

Key Fact

Metals below carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by reduction with carbon (heating the oxide with carbon). Metals above carbon must be extracted by electrolysis. The choice of method depends entirely on the metal’s reactivity relative to carbon.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Predicting Chemical Reactions — Groups and Trends
chemistry-paper-2.description: Properties of Groups 1, 7 and 0, electron arrangement and trends in reactivity.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
The Periodic Table and Groups

The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of atomic number. Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of outer-shell electrons, which is why they have similar chemical properties. Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of electron shells. Mendeleev’s original table was based on atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements. His predictions about these missing elements were later confirmed, validating the periodic arrangement. The table was subsequently refined using atomic number (not atomic mass) as the fundamental organising principle, which resolved anomalies where elements would have been placed in the wrong group if ordered by mass alone.

Group 1 — The Alkali Metals

Group 1 elements (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, francium) are called the alkali metals. They all have one electron in their outer shell, which they lose easily to form +1 ions. They are soft metals that can be cut with a knife, have low melting points compared to most metals, and have low densities — lithium, sodium and potassium all float on water. They must be stored under oil to prevent them reacting with moisture and oxygen in the air.

Group 1 metals react with water to produce a metal hydroxide (an alkaline solution, hence “alkali metals”) and hydrogen gas. For example: \(2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)\). Lithium fizzes gently, sodium melts into a ball and fizzes vigorously, and potassium reacts so vigorously it catches fire with a lilac flame. Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons, making it easier to lose.

Key Fact

Group 1: reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus, more shielded, so easier to lose. Melting points decrease down the group.

Group 7 — The Halogens

Group 7 elements (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine) are called the halogens. They have seven electrons in their outer shell and need to gain one more electron to achieve a full outer shell, forming −1 ions. They exist as diatomic molecules (\(F_2\), \(Cl_2\), \(Br_2\), \(I_2\)). Halogens react with metals to form ionic compounds called halide salts (e.g. sodium chloride, NaCl) and react with non-metals to form covalent compounds.

Physical properties change down the group as the molecules get larger and intermolecular forces become stronger: fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is a green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a grey solid that sublimes to form a purple vapour. Melting and boiling points increase down the group. Reactivity decreases going down Group 7 because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker and it is harder to gain that extra electron.

A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt. For example, chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide solution: \(Cl_2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) \rightarrow 2KCl(aq) + Br_2(aq)\). The solution changes from colourless to orange-brown as bromine is released. Similarly, chlorine displaces iodine from potassium iodide, turning the solution brown. However, bromine cannot displace chlorine from potassium chloride because bromine is less reactive than chlorine. These displacement reactions provide experimental evidence for the reactivity trend.

Group 0 — The Noble Gases

Group 0 elements (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon) are the noble gases. They have full outer electron shells, which makes them very stable and unreactive. They exist as individual atoms (monatomic) rather than molecules because they have no tendency to share, gain or lose electrons. Boiling points increase down the group as the atoms become larger and intermolecular forces increase.

Noble gases are used where unreactive gases are needed: helium for balloons and airships (low density, non-flammable), neon in advertising signs (produces a distinctive red-orange glow when electricity passes through it), and argon in light bulbs and welding (prevents oxidation of the hot filament or metal).

Key Fact

Noble gases are unreactive because they have complete outer electron shells. They do not need to form bonds. Boiling points increase down the group as atomic size and intermolecular forces increase.

Going down any group, atoms have more electron shells. In Group 1, the single outer electron is progressively further from the positive nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons — so it is easier to remove (lose), making the element more reactive. In Group 7, the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker — making it harder to gain an electron, so reactivity decreases. In Group 0, the full outer shell provides stability regardless of size, so all noble gases are unreactive. These trends can be explained entirely by the electronic structure of the atoms. Understanding this pattern means you can predict the properties of any element from its position in the periodic table, even if you have never studied it before.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Identifying Substances
chemistry-paper-2.description: Flame tests, gas tests, and chemical analysis techniques for identifying unknown substances.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
Why We Need Chemical Tests

Chemists often need to identify unknown substances. This might be to check whether a water supply is safe, to identify minerals in rocks, to verify the purity of a manufactured product, or to analyse an unknown sample in a forensic investigation. The OCR Gateway specification requires you to know several key tests that can identify specific ions and gases. These tests fall into two broad categories: traditional wet chemistry tests that rely on visible observations, and modern instrumental methods that use machines for faster, more accurate results.

Flame Tests

A flame test identifies metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen burner flame. Different metal ions emit light of different colours because their electrons absorb energy and then release it as visible light at characteristic wavelengths. To carry out a flame test: dip a clean nichrome wire loop in concentrated hydrochloric acid (to remove previous residues), then dip it into the sample, and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame. The wire must be cleaned thoroughly between tests to avoid contamination from previous samples, which would give misleading results.

Key Fact

Flame test colours: Lithium — crimson red. Sodium — yellow. Potassium — lilac. Calcium — orange-red. Copper — green / blue-green.

Tests for Gases

You must be able to test for four gases. Each test produces a unique, easily identifiable result:

Hydrogen (\(H_2\)) — hold a burning splint near the mouth of the test tube; a squeaky pop confirms hydrogen. The pop is caused by the hydrogen igniting and reacting with oxygen in the air: \(2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\). Oxygen (\(O_2\)) — insert a glowing splint into the gas; it relights because oxygen supports combustion. Carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)) — bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution); it turns milky or cloudy because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed: \(Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O\). Chlorine (\(Cl_2\)) — hold damp litmus paper near the gas; it is first turned red (because chlorine is acidic) and then bleached white because chlorine is a powerful bleaching agent.

Testing for Metal Ions Using Sodium Hydroxide

Adding sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH) to solutions containing metal ions produces coloured precipitates. The precipitate forms because the metal ions react with hydroxide ions to produce an insoluble metal hydroxide. The colour of the precipitate identifies the metal ion present. This is a key practical skill for the exam.

Calcium ions (\(Ca^{2+}\)) — white precipitate of calcium hydroxide. Copper(II) ions (\(Cu^{2+}\)) — blue precipitate of copper hydroxide. Iron(II) ions (\(Fe^{2+}\)) — green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide; the equation is \(Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2\). Iron(III) ions (\(Fe^{3+}\)) — brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide; the equation is \(Fe^{3+} + 3OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_3\). Aluminium ions (\(Al^{3+}\)) — white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution (aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric). Magnesium ions (\(Mg^{2+}\)) — white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH. This difference between aluminium and magnesium is important: both give white precipitates, but only aluminium’s dissolves in excess.

Testing for Negative Ions

You can test for certain negative ions (anions) using specific reagents:

Carbonate ions (\(CO_3^{2-}\)) — add dilute acid (such as hydrochloric acid) to the sample. If carbonates are present, the acid reacts to produce carbon dioxide gas, which can be tested by bubbling it through limewater — it turns milky if \(CO_2\) is present. Sulfate ions (\(SO_4^{2-}\)) — first add dilute hydrochloric acid to remove any carbonate ions that might interfere, then add barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate (\(BaSO_4\)) confirms sulfate ions are present. Halide ions — first add dilute nitric acid (to remove other ions that might interfere), then add silver nitrate solution. Chloride ions (\(Cl^-\)) give a white precipitate of silver chloride, bromide ions (\(Br^-\)) give a cream precipitate of silver bromide, and iodide ions (\(I^-\)) give a yellow precipitate of silver iodide.

Key Fact

Halide tests with silver nitrate: chloride \(\rightarrow\) white precipitate, bromide \(\rightarrow\) cream precipitate, iodide \(\rightarrow\) yellow precipitate. Always acidify with dilute nitric acid first to prevent interference from other ions.

When identifying an unknown ionic compound, work systematically. First dissolve the sample in water. Use a flame test to identify the metal ion (cation). Then use precipitate tests with NaOH to confirm the metal ion. Next, test for the negative ion (anion) using the appropriate reagent — silver nitrate for halides, barium chloride for sulfates, or dilute acid for carbonates. Record all observations carefully and compare with known results.

Instrumental Methods

Instrumental methods of analysis are faster, more sensitive and more accurate than traditional chemical tests. Gas chromatography separates the components of a mixture by passing it through a column; each component travels at a different rate, producing separate peaks on a chromatogram. The number of peaks tells you how many components are in the mixture, and the retention time identifies each substance. Mass spectrometry gives the relative molecular mass of a substance by measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of its ions. Gas chromatography linked with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is particularly powerful because it both separates and identifies components in a single analysis. These methods are used in forensic science, environmental monitoring, drug testing and the pharmaceutical industry.

Instrumental methods can detect very small quantities of a substance (high sensitivity), making them invaluable when only a trace amount is available. They are fast and can be automated for processing many samples. They give accurate, quantitative results rather than just qualitative observations. However, the equipment is expensive to purchase and maintain, and requires trained operators to interpret the data correctly. Despite these costs, instrumental analysis has largely replaced traditional tests in professional laboratories.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Rates of Reaction
chemistry-paper-2.description: Measuring reaction rates, collision theory, and factors affecting rate of reaction.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
What Is Rate of Reaction?

The rate of reaction tells us how quickly a reaction happens — how fast the reactants are used up or how fast the products are formed. A fast reaction (like an explosion) is over in a fraction of a second. A slow reaction (like rusting or the weathering of stone) may take months or years. Being able to control the rate of a reaction is vital in industry — too fast can be dangerous, too slow is uneconomical.

You can measure rate in several ways: the volume of gas produced per unit time, the mass of reactant lost per unit time (using a balance), or the time taken for a colour change or for a solution to become opaque (disappearing cross experiment). The choice of method depends on the particular reaction and what can be conveniently measured.

Collision Theory

Collision theory states that for a reaction to occur, the reacting particles must: (1) collide with each other, (2) collide with sufficient energy (at least the activation energy), and (3) collide with the correct orientation. The rate of reaction depends on the frequency of successful collisions — collisions that have enough energy and the right orientation to result in a reaction. Not every collision leads to a reaction; most collisions are unsuccessful because the particles bounce off each other without reacting.

Key Fact

For a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy) and the correct orientation. Increasing the frequency of successful collisions increases the rate of reaction.

Factors Affecting Rate

Four main factors affect the rate of a chemical reaction:

Temperature — increasing the temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more frequently. More importantly, a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or exceeding the activation energy, so the rate increases significantly.

Concentration (or pressure for gases) — increasing the concentration means there are more particles in a given volume, so they collide more frequently. For gases, increasing the pressure pushes particles closer together, having the same effect.

Surface area — breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases the surface area to volume ratio. More of the solid is exposed to the other reactant, so collisions happen more frequently and the rate increases. This is why powdered marble chips react faster with acid than large lumps, even though the total mass of marble is the same. In the extreme case, a fine powder of a combustible material in air can cause a dust explosion because the surface area is so enormous that the reaction rate is dangerously fast.

Interpreting Rate of Reaction Graphs

Rate graphs typically plot volume of gas produced (or mass lost) on the y-axis against time on the x-axis. The gradient (steepness) of the line shows the rate — a steeper gradient means a faster reaction. The line levels off when one of the reactants is used up (the reaction is complete). The final amount of product is the same regardless of rate (unless the amount of reactant changes). Two curves on the same graph — one steep and one gradual — that level off at the same point indicate the same amount of reactant was used but one reaction was faster than the other.

You can also use \(\frac{1}{t}\) as a measure of rate, where \(t\) is the time taken for a certain amount of reaction to occur. A shorter time means a faster rate, so \(\frac{1}{t}\) is proportional to rate.

Catalysts

A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up itself. It works by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more particles have enough energy to react. On a reaction profile, the catalyst lowers the energy barrier (the peak). The catalyst itself is unchanged at the end of the reaction and can be reused. Each catalyst is specific to a particular reaction or type of reaction — an iron catalyst works for the Haber process but not for decomposing hydrogen peroxide (which uses manganese dioxide).

Key Fact

Catalysts speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. They are not used up and are not changed permanently. Different reactions need different catalysts. Enzymes are biological catalysts that control reactions in living organisms.

Gas syringe method: collect gas produced in a gas syringe and record the volume at regular time intervals. Works well for reactions producing \(CO_2\) or \(H_2\) (e.g. marble chips and acid, magnesium and acid). Mass loss method: place the reaction on a balance and record the mass at regular intervals as gas escapes. Disappearing cross: time how long it takes for a cross viewed through the solution to disappear as the solution becomes opaque (sodium thiosulfate and acid producing sulfur). In all methods, change only one variable at a time and keep everything else constant.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Equilibria
chemistry-paper-2.description: Reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium, and Le Chatelier's principle.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
Reversible Reactions

Most chemical reactions go to completion — the reactants are used up and only products remain. However, some reactions are reversible. In a reversible reaction, the products can react to re-form the original reactants. This is shown by the equilibrium symbol \(\rightleftharpoons\) instead of a single arrow. Many important industrial and biological reactions are reversible, and understanding how to control them is essential for maximising product yield in chemical manufacturing.

For example, the decomposition of ammonium chloride: \(NH_4Cl(s) \rightleftharpoons NH_3(g) + HCl(g)\). When heated, ammonium chloride breaks down into ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases. When cooled, these gases recombine to form solid ammonium chloride again. The forward reaction is endothermic (absorbs energy); the reverse reaction is exothermic (releases energy). Another example is the reaction of hydrated copper sulfate: blue \(CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O\) turns white (anhydrous \(CuSO_4\)) when heated, and turns blue again when water is added.

Key Fact

In a reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic (and vice versa). The energy change in each direction has the same magnitude but opposite sign.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system (where nothing can enter or leave), a dynamic equilibrium is eventually reached. At equilibrium, three conditions are met:

• The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.

• The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but not necessarily equal to each other).

• Both reactions are still occurring at the molecular level — this is why it is called “dynamic.” Molecules are continuously reacting in both directions, but the overall proportions do not change.

Equilibrium does not mean the amounts of reactants and products are equal — it means they are constant. The equilibrium position can favour the products (more products than reactants) or the reactants (more reactants than products). Also, equilibrium is not a static state — both reactions continue at equal rates, like two escalators running in opposite directions at the same speed. You can only achieve equilibrium in a closed system; in an open system, products can escape and equilibrium is never reached.

Le Chatelier’s Principle (Higher)
